00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.name: Constitution of the Slav-Macedonian Scientific and Literary Society in Saint Petersburg
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.short_description: The Slav-Macedonian Scientific Literary Society was established in St. Petersburg on 16 December 1903, acting under the patronage of the St. Petersburg Slav Charitable Society. Its founders were Krste Petkov Misirkov (1874–1926) and Dimitija Chupovski, who worked actively on the recognition of Macedonian as distinct Slavic language and the opening of native-language schools for children in Macedonia. The Society, also known as the Macedonian Colony in St. Petersburg, gathered many distinguished Macedonian writers, poets and publicists. Its extensive scientific and literary activities have brought about explicit formulation of the Macedonian national program. The Society largely contributed to issuing a periodical publication in Macedonian and Russian language called “Makedonski Golos” (“Macedonian Voice"). It played an important role in the national awakening of Macedonians and bringing forth the issue of the Macedonian autonomy in the international community.
00a5042b-0fd6-51a0-9c1e-ba80caedf302.holder: University of St. Cyril and Methodius - Publisher

00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.name: Société des Fermes Françaises de Tunisie
00dac457-85a0-5a63-aebd-676267b9816c.short_description: French agriculture in Tunisia came about either through the establishment of large properties by private initiatives, or the arrangement of settlers by the public authorities. This is a text from the "first phase" - one of the "companies" (of "French farms") had purchased a large plot of land, and employed a number of (largely Arab and Italian) workers to cultivate it. It aims to publicise the company and make it attractive to both prospective immigrants to tunisia, and attract funds.

00eecee6-1a79-5ca4-885a-64eb797adc19.name: *The bas-reliefs of Trajan's Column, reproduced in electroplating and exhibited in a room of the new Louvre*
00eecee6-1a79-5ca4-885a-64eb797adc19.short_description: Trajan's Column, erected in Rome, is famous for its exceptional bas-reliefs commemorating the victory of the Emperor over the Dacians. In 1861, with the aim of making it known to the French public, Napoléon III had the column moulded and a replica installed in Paris. This was achieved thanks to the new electroplating technique, and the copy was placed in the Musée du Louvre. However, in 1870 the column was judged too large, and was sent to the Château de Saint-Germain, where it was quickly installed in the moat. In this image shows visitors at the Louvre, examining the story reproduced by Trajan's Column.

01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.name: Omar Pasha (1806–1871)
01425452-ab97-5882-bfb1-7f4f896ba157.short_description: Portrait of Omar Pasha. He was born in Croatia in 1806 near the Turkish-Hungarian border. In 1828 he deserted from the Austrian army and joined the Ottoman administration in Bosnia. After a long career in the Ottoman army, he became the military governor of Bucharest and commanded the Ottoman forces at the siege of Sevastopol in Crimea. In 1862 he suppressed an uprising in Herzogovina and led a victorious campaign against Montenegro. In 1868 he became War Minister and died in 1871 in Istanbul.
keywords: Omar Pasha; Croatia; Bosnia; Ottoman empire; Herzegovina

01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.name: [Paris] stock exchange
01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.short_description: This building (Palais Brongniart), located in the heart of Paris, housed the French stock exchange for almost two centuries. Its atmosphere, as a powerful financial building bearing witness to great bankers' fortunes and failures, inspired writers such as Honoré de Balzac in La Maison Nucingen and Émile Zola in L’Argent.

02aa485b-b3bc-53cc-91c5-b9f267c8d3b1.name: *Constantinople et le Bosphore de Thrace*
02aa485b-b3bc-53cc-91c5-b9f267c8d3b1.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.name: The Coffee Shop of Cairo
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.short_description: This colourful print depicts a typical 19th century coffeeshop in Cairo. An exclusively male domain, its design was characterised by an open front and wide benches for seating, to allow for easy congregation and the gathering of friends and acquainances. Not only in Cairo, which had over a thousands coffeehouses in Roberts's time, but all over the Middle East, coffeehouses were important social hubs for the exchange of news, entertainment, smoking (customers brought their own pipes and waterpipes) and - not rarely - political dissent. Musicians and storytellers often enhanced the experience further. In this image, the proprietor or an employee of the cafe can be seen serving a beverage in the centre. Interestingly, both the ewer and the large copper cup he uses are of a type usually associated with water, not coffee. Perhaps Roberts introduced these items for artistic effect.

03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.name: Construction Site at Shellal
03110c09-4d62-5959-a659-ea8534ac6e28.short_description: In 1900, Count Giulio d’Aspremont, an Italian diplomat, visited the construction site of the first dam across the Nile (today known as the Aswan Low Dam or Old Aswan Dam). He took several pictures of the works and of the monuments on the island of Philae that were going to be submerged by the water. He published some of them on the *Bulletin of the Italian Geographical Society*, where he wrote that up to 2,000 Italian workers were employed in the works (as stone-cutters, miners and masons), out of a total labour force of about 10,000 or 12,000; an Italian village had sprung up on the Nile banks, with modest little houses, trattorias and shops.

036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.name: An Italian cartoon in support of Ahmad Urabi's movement against foreign control of Egypt's finances
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.short_description:
Ahmad Urabi was an Egyptian colonel of peasant origins who led a revolt in 1879-1882 aimed at eliminating foreign control of Egyptian finances and establishing constitutional limits to the Khedive’s authority. John Bull is a recognized national personification of the United Kingdom.  
Caption: “Be careful, merchant! Despite your cannons, your ships and your money, I will be able to teach you that in places where true love for one’s country flourishes, people can make heroic miracles in order to defend their homeland!”  
Part of the Italian public opinion sided with the Egyptians, against the British, since it likened Egyptian struggle with Italian struggle for national unification and self-determination. Ironically, however, in 1882 Italy occupied Massawa, on the Red Sea, and started its own colonial expansion.
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
036c65ce-1ec4-519a-9780-ee407c279d2e.author: Giulia Barrera

036f240e-d388-502f-b085-dcd2a8068418.name: Rashid Pasha Mustafa Mehmet (1802–1858)
036f240e-d388-502f-b085-dcd2a8068418.short_description: Portrait of Rashid Pasha. He was born in 1800 in Istanbul and joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at the age of 20. He served as Ottoman Ambassador in Paris and London. In 1837 he became Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Ottoman Empire. In 1838 he lost his position, but still negotiated as a Turkish diplomat in London, Paris and Berlin. In 1846 he became Grand Vizier and initiated a number of reforms.

04456e8e-b665-5aa7-96a4-825dc6689071.name: Near Eastern and Balkan map
04456e8e-b665-5aa7-96a4-825dc6689071.short_description: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. Abdülhamid II was the 34th Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and the last Sultan to exert effective autocratic control over the fracturing state. He oversaw a period of decline in the power and extent of the empire, including widespread pogroms and government massacres against the minorities of the empire (named the Hamidian massacres, after him) as well as an assassination attempt. He ruled from 31 August 1876 until he was deposed shortly after the 1908 Young Turk Revolution, on 27 April 1909.
04456e8e-b665-5aa7-96a4-825dc6689071.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.name: Alexandria: The Consuls’ Square Rebuilt
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.short_description: The large, rectangular square initially know under the French name “Place des Consuls” (later as Muhammad 'Ali Square), was officially inaugurated in 1860. It was designed by Francesco Mancini, chief engineer of the “Commissione d’ornato” (Board of Works), a committee set up in 1834 by Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt in 1805-1848), and modelled after similar urban-planning committees already functioning in some Italian cities. In 1872, an equestrian statue of Muhammad 'Ali was erected in the square, which took his name. In July 1882, after anti-foreign rioting in Alexandria, the British fleet heavily bombed the city, causing major destructions to the buildings surrounding the square.
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera

07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.name: Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico “L. Pigorini” (National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography), Exhibition Room
07024cd6-c5bb-5d57-96ec-903ad7f248c4.short_description:
The origins, in terms of scientific activity and conservation, of the Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the “Regio Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico di Roma" (Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography). Initially the museum was located in a wing of the Palazzo del Collegio Romano built in the late 16th century by the Society of Jesus.  
This rare image represents the old arrangement of one of the rooms of the Roman College, where the collection of antiquities and curiosities gathered together by Father Athanasius Kircher was kept after the foundation of the museum. According to the intentions of its founder, Luigi Pigorini, the purpose of this new institution was not only to gather together the remains of Italian prehistoric culture and the "primitive" cultures of other European and non-European peoples in a "central" museum located in the new capital of the Kingdom, but above all to support, promote and participate in research by paleontologists in Italy.

0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.name: The drawings of Janissary clothes from The Album of Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniye (The collection of Ottoman Pictures)
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.short_description: Arif Mehmed Pasha is considered one of the leaders of the western style of painting in Turkey. He developed a talent for drawing and produced a series of pictures detailing the clothes Ottoman state officials wore. He prepared these pictures under the name *Mecmua-i Tesavir-i Osmaniyye*. Although his work was supposed to come out in 12 volumes, only one volume was actually published in French in Paris in 1863 and in Turkish the same year. The other 11 volumes have been lost. The published volume is considered to be the first illustrated book in Turkey. What is amazing is the praise heaped onto Arif Mehmed Pasha for his portraits, the harmony of their colours and tones, the maturity of attitude and delicate detail, the artist’s control over his pen and watercolours. The clothing reflects the time when the Janissaries were still on the scene (before 1826 when the corps was disbanded).
0801264d-8475-5c87-a800-17b6d0cc190e.holder: Military Museum and Cultural Centre Command

08d3aed6-3599-5046-816b-66df7858d6a8.name: *The Sultan’s Horses* (Drawing 19 for the *XX Dessins* album)
08d3aed6-3599-5046-816b-66df7858d6a8.description: This drawing by Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso forms part of an album, *XX Dessins*, which was published in 1912 and represents a key point of breakthrough for the artist. The context of the work can be explained by his interest in the Western primitivists, the influence of African art, the experiences that he exchanged with Brancusi and Modigliani, and his study of Henri Rousseau’s work. The artist aims to present a demarcated image of his own identity: in an elegantly sophisticated picture replete with medieval imagery, he produces an original work that explores volumes, dynamic forms, and the sense of speed. It was this clearly defined image that Amadeo presented at the Armory Show in 1913, where his work achieved great success in both critical and market terms.
08d3aed6-3599-5046-816b-66df7858d6a8.holder: Modern Art Centre, Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation

091c2bb3-6009-5f5c-bff2-8e5c54938f6c.name: *Chancel of the Church of St Helena*
091c2bb3-6009-5f5c-bff2-8e5c54938f6c.short_description: The slightly confusing title of this print by David Roberts actually refers to the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, first commissioned in 327 AD by the Emperor Constantine and his mother Helena. at the spot where it is believed Jesus was born. The view captures the area before the iconostasis shielding the main altar in the eastern apse of the church, as well as - below on the right - the south-eastern entrance to the Grotto of the Nativity.The Church of the Nativity is one of the foremost pilgrimage sites for Christians and would have been a highlight on the itinerary of European travellers to the Holy Land. As is typical for his works, Roberts exaggerates the proportions of the architecture in relation to the human figures, which appear dwarfed by the majesty and monumentality of the structures that surround them.

0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.name: *The Religious Pilgrimage of the Mohammadans - Makkah (Arabia) - General View of the City, the Precinct and Enclosure of the Al-Haram Mosque and the Holy Kaaba*
0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.short_description: This print was originally published in 'La Ilustracion Espanola y Americana', a newspaper published in Madrid on the 15th of April, 1882. Entitled 'La Peregrinacion religiosa de los mahometanos: Vista general de la Meca, del patio y claustro de la mesquita El-Haram y de la Santa Kaaba', it was copied from the first known photograph (at the time) depicting the Makkah precinct, taken - according to the newspaper - by the English traveller Mr [John Fryer Thomas] Keane.  Keane (1854-1937) was a clergyman, who converted to Islam and visited Makkah in 1877. In 1881, he published two books about his experiences in the Hijaz, 'Six Months in Meccah' and 'My Journey to Medinah'. The image shows the courtyard of the Makkah mosque with hundreds of pilgrims clustering around the Ka'bah at the centre. Beyond, the hills of Makkah with their traditional houses, many of them multistoreyed, can be seen.

0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.name: *Mount Tabor*
0a226934-adb7-5611-ac1e-769b4276935b.short_description: This depiction of Mount Tabor by the American artist John Douglas Woodward carries the caption 'Mount Tabor. Bearing among the Arabs, like so many other mountains, only the general name 'Jebel et Tur'. The scene suggests a rugged, primeval landscape untouched by modern humanity, the mystically lit, driven clouds that half veil the mounting evoking a spiritual and at the same time awe-inspiring atmosphere well suited to an important biblical site. In popular Christian tradition: Mount Tabor was associated with the Transfiguration of Christ. At the same time the mountain was to prove of historical importance, too.  In 1799, during the time of Napoleon Bonaparte's expedition in the area, the valley between Mount Tabor and the Moreh Hill saw a decisive battle in which a French force of about 3,000 soldiers under the command of Napoleon and General Jean Baptiste Kléber faced a Mamluk force of about 20,000 soldiers.

0b654295-705f-5779-91d5-6ee361403ebb.name: Nouvelle gare de Haidar-Pacha. (New Haidar Pasha Station)
0b654295-705f-5779-91d5-6ee361403ebb.description: The postcard depicts the new Haidar-Pasha station, Constantinople. The first station before the new one was a modest structure appropriate to a relatively short suburban and regional railway. As the network expanded across Anatolia and the planning of the Baghdad Railway, the construction of the present station began in 1906. The architects were Otto Ritter and Hellmuth Cuno, and construction was undertaken by the German firm Philipp Holzmann. The station is a Neoclassical building that draws its symmetrical monumental composition, steep roofs, towers, stone façades and architectural vocabulary from European historicism. The postcard presents the station from the Bosporus, emphasising its monumental waterside façade. The building occupies an artificial platform at the edge of the sea and functions as an intermodal transport complex linking trains, ferries and port installations.

0b7f2149-f01d-5891-815e-947600259db6.name: *The drilling of an artesian well*
0b7f2149-f01d-5891-815e-947600259db6.short_description: The purpose of the album *Les Colonies Françaises* was to highlight, amongst other things, the French "achievements" and technological innovations in the colonies, and thus legitimise their rule. This image shows the construction of an artesian well in Tunisia in the 19th century. In reality, however, this type of well was built by the French army in order to appease the populations in agricultural areas and thus better control them.

0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.name: The fundamental pact
0b914ea4-3750-5949-ba83-6be97904425d.short_description: This foundational text was drawn up by Mohamed Bey of the Husainid dynasty (1855–1859) under the pressure of the French and English consuls. They had the aim of either adopting or adapting the reforms introduced in Istanbul which required them to provide non-Muslim subjects with semi-secular services, such as the establishment of mixed tribunals avoiding the strict application of the Quran, and also ensured free trade for France and England.

0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.name: *Raft Conveying Winged Bull to Baghdad*
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.short_description: Layard describes the removal of the winged bulls from the site of the mound of Nimrud in Nineveh and its remains, 1849, from where they had lain for approximately the last 2,730 years. They were carefully loaded on to rafts, made in the traditional way of using hundreds of inflated goat and sheep-skins supporting a wooden superstructure. Layard (who had learnt Arabic and Persian) recruited the crew locally, as he had done with his workforce. In April 1847, he sent them floating with the current, off on a six hundred mile journey down the river Tigris to Basra, where ships of the British Navy were waiting to take them the next 12,000 miles to England. Although the artist Cooper was not present on this occasion, he subsequently witnessed similar events, and would have been able to reconstruct the scene.
0bdb3920-5c44-5859-a7de-be6f63a099b9.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

0c6aabc0-aac2-5d65-82f5-b3a3f1826243.name: *Senator Ratta Banquet*
0c6aabc0-aac2-5d65-82f5-b3a3f1826243.description:
In this sumptuous installation which was organised by Francesco Ratta theatrical baroque pomp is evident. At the end of his charge, lasting two months, each Gonfaloniere had to offer a banquet at his expenses to his colleagues (the Anziani). It was a good occasion for exhibiting grandiosity, riches and celebrating family prestige, even if these heavy expenses were ultimately fatal to personal finances.  
This spectacular banquet is documented by a series of eight prints. They portray the decoration of the open gallery with garlands and depict details of some of the interior decorations. The room in the residence once owned by the Vizzani family (nowadays Sanguinetti, Via S. Stefano, 43) has as its centerpiece a spectacular sugar trophy designed by the sculptor Giuseppe Maria Mazza: one-meter-high, wrought after the techniques of the glass masters of Murano by the confectioner Giovan Battista Zacarini. It is a surprisingly rocky mountain made of silver and veiled in green, reflective of the famous Bernini fountain in Piazza Navona, it is surrounded by the allegorical statues of the four rivers. From their urns is an outpouring of delicious food. This space is encompassed by a great table for 66 guests, which because of its round shape priority problems were averted. The room scenography bears the family heraldic symbols. Golden griffins and palm leaves clearly allude to the prosperity of Bologna during the government of Francesco Ratta. Along the green damask covered walls small mirrors are hung, tilted to multiply the original and artistic compositions of bottles and precious plates which are scattered all over. The Hall, painted by Tommaso Laureti (n. 1530 – m. 1602), shows in the middle of the ceiling *Victory Presenting Fame with the World Conquered by Alexander the Great* and a frieze with Alexander's adventures successively covered by new decorations.
0c6aabc0-aac2-5d65-82f5-b3a3f1826243.short_description: At the end of his charge as a Gonfaloniere (the most significant political position occupied in turns every two months by the Bolognese senators until the age of Napoleon), Francesco Ratta offered the Anziani a memorable banquet. On this occasion, the Hall of his residence was transformed thanks to a baroque ephemera set documented by this series of etchings and a printed description.
0c6aabc0-aac2-5d65-82f5-b3a3f1826243.provenance: The print is part of the series *Disegni del convito fatto dall'illustrissimo Signor Senatore Francesco Ratta all’Illustrissimo Publico, Eccelsi Signori Anziani, & altra Nobiltà terminando il suo Confalonierato Li 28 Febraro 1693*, (*Drawings of the banquet organized by the most illustrious senator Francesco Ratta to the most illustrious, distinguished and noble public including the supreme Anziani, and other noblemen to celebrate the end of his Gonfalonierato the 28th of February 1693*), In Bologna, Per li Peri All’Angelo Custode, 1693

0cbc7e1b-2d6c-5b8a-a3c2-1ce733f00a89.name: Etching showing the so called Museo Cospiano in Bologna
0cbc7e1b-2d6c-5b8a-a3c2-1ce733f00a89.description: Illustrating the book by Lorenzo Legati entitled *Museo Cospiano* (Bologna 1677) this etching shows the interior of the museum owned by Marquis Ferdinando Cospi. Officially bequeathed to the city in 1672 the museum was housed in the Palazzo Pubblico along with the naturalistic collection of Ulisse Aldrovandi since 1657. The text describes the exhibits: things living on the earth, in the sea, fossils (*naturalia*), and artefacts such as coins and medals, sculptures, small bronzes and archaeological relics (*artificialia*). Some of the objects represented here are still recognizable among those surviving in the city museums. Among the *Mirabilia* there was also the “dimostratore”, a guide who was a dwarf. This collection is a good example of the XVII century encyclopaedic taste and seems to be inspired more by curiosity and wonder than by genuine scientific interest. It grew progressively thanks to contacts and exchanges with travellers and correspondents abroad. After having been moved to the Institute of Sciences in Palazzo Poggi in 1743 the Cospi collection was used for a didactic inspired by the Enlightenment ideas and based on a direct experience of materials. Following the Napoleonic suppressions and a crisis for the institute there was a new distribution and reclassification of materials in the age of Positivism. The collection was divided among different Museums in Bologna based on their subject or scientific field. Several of the pieces in the American Collection were bought by Luigi Pigorini in the 19th century and are now housed in the Pigorini Museum, in Rome.
0cbc7e1b-2d6c-5b8a-a3c2-1ce733f00a89.short_description: Marquis Ferdinado Cospi’s *Wunderkammer* is a good example of the encyclopedic collections fashionable in Europe in the Baroque age. It was composed of *Naturalia and Mirabilia*, a combination of items coming from the world of nature, antiquity, artifacts and scientific instruments.
0cbc7e1b-2d6c-5b8a-a3c2-1ce733f00a89.owner: Biblioteca Comunale dell'Archiginnasio, Comune di Bologna

0dd30a0a-1b26-5aa8-95ed-2abdad17a184.name: *Tercüman-ı Ahval* Newspaper
0dd30a0a-1b26-5aa8-95ed-2abdad17a184.short_description: *Tercüman-ı Ahvâl* was the first private newspaper published in Istanbul. It was produced between 1860-1866 by Agah Efendi and Şinasi, men of letters of Tanzimat Era. Initially it was published only on Sundays, but starting from the 25th issue in 1861, it was published three times a week. Leading authors of the period such as Ahmed Vefik Paşa, Ziya Paşa and Refik Bey frequently wrote for it, discussing the reasons for the backwardness of Ottoman society and current events. In the paper, works of literature were also published. For instance the first Turkish theatre play, *Wedding/Marriage* of the Poet, by Şinasi (1860) was published as a series. The paper was closed for two weeks in 1861 after a very critical article probably written by Ziya Paşa. This is regarded as the first example of a ban in Turkish press. The paper was no longer published after 11 March 1866.

0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.name: *The Bridge Carol I*
0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.short_description: The railroad bridge over the Danube that was built between 1890–1895 in South-Eastern Romania shortened the route of the Orient Express, a passenger train meant to connect Paris to Istanbul. The bridge made it possible for the Orient Express to reach Constanţa, a Black Sea port, from where ships went to Istanbul, whereas in the past the journey implied people being ferried on the Danube from Romania to Bulgaria, travelling by train to Varna (a Bulgarian Black Sea port) and then taking a ship to Istanbul. The “Carol I” bridge, which was designed by engineer Anghel Saligny and was at that time the longest in Europe, was inaugurated on 29 September 1895. In his inaugural speech, the king declared that “Romania is now owner of the shortest route between the northern seas and the countries of the Orient”.

0e6a50b3-2b5c-5608-aae5-77ecf66cfde2.name: *Sketch of Algeria, featuring the Roman occupation, the railway lines, roads suitable for mule and horse drawn vehicles, ports* \[…\] drawn from an archaeological point of view and dedicated to ...
0e6a50b3-2b5c-5608-aae5-77ecf66cfde2.short_description: Founded in 1856, the Société Historique Algérienne organised excavations, published a journal, and created maps and plans. This map helped facilitate research on the Roman occupation of Algeria, by indicating clearly the main sites, how to get there, and other elements which allow the reader to better understand the Roman presence (such as marble quarries and thermal baths).

0e85d24e-665e-5157-bf0e-e0f313fbe465.name: Air Orient Company. Planisphere. Weekly Air Service France-Syria-Indochina
0e85d24e-665e-5157-bf0e-e0f313fbe465.description: This 1930s Air Orient poster highlights the French airline’s east–west routes across the Middle East. From Beirut and Damascus to Baghdad and Basra, the service carried passengers and mail between Paris and the Levant. Produced in a republican France that was also a vast colonial empire, the poster embodies both the allure of modern aviation and the projection of French influence through new networks of mobility.

0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.name: *Egypt. Suez canal.*
0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.short_description: The inauguration of the Suez Canal saw spectacular celebrations, attended by many European royalties. This was a huge victory for Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had sincerely hoped it would be a memorable and historical event. On his request, the painter Édouard Riou (1833–1900) produced a series of watercolours which were later published in *L’Album de l’Impératrice : Voyage Pittoresque à travers l’Isthme de Suez*.
keywords: Suez canal; Egypt; Ferdinand de Lesseps

0ef1fad2-ddb0-571e-aa44-e858e5b159ac.name: *Die stadt Algier*
0ef1fad2-ddb0-571e-aa44-e858e5b159ac.short_description: According to the historiographer Gabriel Esquer, this illustration was the most detailed view of Algiers available in the 17th century. The artist has accurately mapped out the streets and houses of the city.

0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.name: The Italian Politeama Rossini theatre in Tunis, inaugurated in 1903
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.short_description:
The Politeama Rossini was built by the construction company of Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who had migrated to Tunisia in 1882); the architect was a Mr. Baron. It could house an audience of 2,500.  
The first Italian theatre in Tunis was the “Teatro Tapia” founded in 1826. Other Italian theatres (such as the “Teatro Italiano” and the “Teatro Paradiso”) and concert halls (“Gran Teatro”, “Teatro Cohen”, etc.) were created in Tunis the following decades.
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.author: Giulia Barrera

0f0a80ba-ac59-5cc2-9963-b390e49608d0.short_description: Within the International Exhibition in Paris, 1878, commercial activities typical of the colony were performed in the park next to Trocadero Pavilion. The scene shows the practice of making unfiltered coffee inside a kitchen decorated with *majolicas*, part of the reconstruction of a hypothetical neighbourhood in Algeria.

0f2af30a-b903-5cfa-a52e-5a834629196d.name: *Sbeïtla. Attempt to reconstruct the façade of the three temples*
0f2af30a-b903-5cfa-a52e-5a834629196d.short_description: The French architect and winner of the Grand Prix de Rome, Henri Saladin, went on an archaeological campaign to Tunisia with the archaeologist René Cagnat between 1882 and 1883. He took many sketches in various archaeological sites, such as this drawing of Sbeïtla (the ancient Roman city in Sufetula). Upon his return he constructed a "Tunisian pavilion" for the 1889 Exposition Universelle (world fair) in Paris, which contained a mix of all the different architectural styles he had seen during his time in Tunisia.

104473a3-fc89-55f7-a3b9-20138dba554c.name: Plan of the city of Pompeii and the excavations there, pl. 2. Historical note
104473a3-fc89-55f7-a3b9-20138dba554c.short_description: The architect François Mazois (1783–1826) was appointed as Caroline Murat's official artist in 1809. He was allowed to set up in Pompeii to draw and measure the ruins, something unheard of at this time. His drawings and observations, published under the title *Les Ruines de Pompéi, Dessinées et Mesurées pendant les Années 1809 à 1811*, became a model for contemporary archaeologists and a source of inspiration for neo-Classical architecture.

1057c04c-dcfd-5f86-aac4-e464ef4ed226.name: Diploma awarded to the Vista Alegre factory
1057c04c-dcfd-5f86-aac4-e464ef4ed226.short_description: The participation in commercial exhibitions by the Vista Alegre Factory began in 1838, with the presentation of a glass and crystal collection in the Exhibition promoted by the Portuguese Industrial Society. In 1851 Vista Alegre took part in the Universal Exhibition, organized in London, and again in 1867 in Paris, having won the copper medal. In 1873 the factory received the Medal for Merit in the International Exhibition of Vienna, Austria. Universal Exhibitions represent in the 19th century an excellent medium for commercial and artistic exchanges, as well as a public stage for the competition between. This display arenas, with an international vocation, commercial exhibitions were ideal for the promotion of technical and artistic skills of European industries.
keywords: International Exhibitions; Portugal; Vista Alegre; Factory

10c5da68-3de4-54d1-9e73-5196e05c7ae8.name: *Description de L'Egypte: Antiquités Planches*
10c5da68-3de4-54d1-9e73-5196e05c7ae8.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. The *Description de l'Égypte* was a series of publications, appearing first in 1809 and continuing until the final volume in 1829, which offered a comprehensive scientific description of ancient and modern Egypt as well as its natural history. It is the collaborative work of about 160 civilian scholars and scientists, known popularly as the savants, who accompanied Napoleon's expedition to Egypt in 1798 to 1801 as part of the French Revolutionary Wars, as well as about 2000 artists and technicians, including 400 engravers, who would later compile it into a full work.

10e20816-215a-59c8-b59d-b15f4c933e82.name: Mahmud II Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839)
10e20816-215a-59c8-b59d-b15f4c933e82.short_description:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.
keywords: Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Janissary; Konya; Ibrahim Pasha; Muhammad Ali; Greece

12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.name: Clashes between agricultural labourers on strike and the mounted police in Cerignola (Foggia, Apulia, in southern Italy)
12e1f5c3-c135-5c06-b2c9-4dc99c6e764e.short_description:
Agricultural workers were at the forefront of Italian labour movement. In 1901, they created the National Federation of Agricultural Workers (Federazione nazionale dei lavoratori della terra).  
In 1904, at Cerignola, the police violently repressed a protest of agricultural workers, killing 4 and injuring 40.

131cc02c-dea1-5e00-b932-6c0832f9d8d7.name: *Diligence / Diligentia*
131cc02c-dea1-5e00-b932-6c0832f9d8d7.description:
The drawing is plan-sketch for the side walls of a niche for the Olomouc Town Hall astronomical clock, a tower clock with several chronological devices and pictorial symbolism. It depicts Diligence or Industriousness and Punctuality. Her attributes include a spider spinning a web, an hourglass, a cockerel pecking grain and the placement of the female figure in a cave. One interesting detail is a spur held by the woman: even Diligence needs to be pricked. The motifs are derived from Cesare Ripa's *Iconology*, the most widespread pictorial manual of the period.  
Plan-sketches included a detailed description of the clock, respecting the original 15th-century plan. The decoration, with allegorical scenes of the Seven Liberal Arts, had a markedly secular character. Other scenes comprised Grammar, Mechanics, Arithmetic, Astronomy, Philosophy, Dialectics, Music and Geometry portrayed as female figures with various attributes, supplemented by the figures of the Mathematician, the Astronomer, Apollo, with a Muse, and Pegasus. The series of drawings for the unpreserved parts of the Olomouc clock is one of the highlights of the work of Jan Kryštof Handke, a leading Olomouc artist. He created easel and ceiling paintings in central and north Moravia and east Bohemia. Handke's most important work is the fresco in the auditorium of the Jesuit university in Wroclaw. The Prague astronomical clock and the Olomouc clock are the only ones of their kind preserved in the Czech Republic. As part of the town hall, it demonstrates the significance of Olomouc as the seat of the bishopric and a one-time centre of Moravia. The original appearance of the clock is not preserved, the present one is in the style of *Socialist Realismus* made in the 1950s by Karel Svolinský.
131cc02c-dea1-5e00-b932-6c0832f9d8d7.short_description: The drawing is one of the plan-sketches for the painted decoration of the Olomouc astronomical clock. The allegorical scenes, with the Seven Liberal Arts, had a markedly secular character, demonstrating the significance of Olomouc as the seat of the bishopric and a one-time centre of Moravia.
131cc02c-dea1-5e00-b932-6c0832f9d8d7.method_for_datation: The town council assigned the painted decoration of the restored town hall clock to the Kryštof Handke workshop in 1746; it was executed in the following year. Handke also mentioned the series of 12 planning sketches for the astronomical clock, and their realisation, in his biography.
131cc02c-dea1-5e00-b932-6c0832f9d8d7.obtention: Until the end of the 19th century the drawing was deposited in Olomouc Town Hall. Around 1900 it was found in the German Museum from whence it passed to the municipal archive and later to the district archive.

138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.name: *View of Constantinople*
138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.short_description: Both this print and the *View of Smyrna* are based on earlier Western ones, which have been assimilated into the distinctive Athonite topographical style. They are exceptions to the corpus of Athonite prints, since they are of secular subjects. The printmaker was, indeed, active outside Athos, where he executed nonreligious commissions. The subjects relate to the tradition of topographical murals depicting important commercial and cultural centers of the day that decorated the mansions of wealthy merchants by the mid-eighteenth century. Kaldis aimed to supply a wider public with inexpensive works of a decorative nature. The activity of merchants from Lesbos at Smyrna, Constantinople, and the Black Sea on the one hand justified the choice of subject and, on the other, provided the appropriate network in which the multiple printed works could circulate. In order to attract the largest possible clientele, the view is coloured and annotated with explanatory comments in Greek and Turkish.

14edc45d-6bf0-507b-a305-757f6f034ef5.name: Portrait of Emperor Shah Jahan
14edc45d-6bf0-507b-a305-757f6f034ef5.short_description: The bearded emperor Shah Jahan, with a nimbus around his head, stands facing proper left, holding a flower in his raised left hand, his right clasping the hilt of his sheathed sword, which is pointed toward the ground. He wears a *jama* (a kind of frock with skirt). A *kamarband* (sash with ends pendant) girdles the waist, and a *dupatta* (scarf) falls over the left shoulder, the end dropping to the waist line. A dagger (*kataar*) is stuck in his sash on his waist. On his feet are heelless slippers. *Pajamas* are worn under the *jama*. The emperor also wears a jeweled *pagari* (turban) with the *sarpes* (plume), encircled by a dark halo. The *sarpes* appears to be jeweled. He wears the following jewelry: a *mala* (necklace); a *bhuja* band (armlet); and a *kangana* (bracelet). A tannish-gold thin border with dark-tan floral drawings surrounds the painting. The page background is decorated in a floral motif with feral feline heads in shades of tan and gold.
14edc45d-6bf0-507b-a305-757f6f034ef5.dimensions: Image: Length: 21cm x Width: 12.4cm; Sheet: Length: 34cm x Width: 21.8cm
14edc45d-6bf0-507b-a305-757f6f034ef5.method_for_datation: This miniature painting depicts Emperor Shah Jahan (1592–1666). This border originally belonged to the Persian dictionary Farhang-i-Jahangiri (1608), which was later cut up and its borders added to many Mughal miniatures, such as this one.
14edc45d-6bf0-507b-a305-757f6f034ef5.method_for_provenance: This miniature painting depicts Emperor Shah Jahan (1592–1666) in formal court attire. This painting is one of only four full-length standing portraits of Shah Jahan known.

159f7828-e467-5f3d-b3ba-96aafc6f5b7c.name: Postcard: *Colonial Exhibition 1907, Tuareg caravan*
159f7828-e467-5f3d-b3ba-96aafc6f5b7c.description:
This postcard (not franked or used) is part of a collection donated by the anthropologist Manuel Antón.  
During the second half of the nineteenth century in Europe and America there were held countless ethnological and colonial exhibitions that showed groups of individuals from distant exotic territories, to make them public and available to anthropologists and scholars. They were put on show alongside exotic animals and recreations of the structures inhabited by these people in their places of origin.  
These exhibitions were a result of the intensification of colonial imperialism of the West and also the relative popularity of two young scientific disciplines (physical anthropology and ethnology) and the development of new and intense forms of consumerism among the European bourgeoisie. Actually these exhibitions got to transmit a sense of lower and "savage" status of the colonised people (Sánchez Gómez, L. “Espectáculos demasiado humanos”, 2008, 88-89).

16145c6c-e484-5568-ab55-c93317ec5964.name: Carol I, King of Romania (1839–1914) / Karl von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen
16145c6c-e484-5568-ab55-c93317ec5964.short_description: Portrait of Carol I, King of Romania (1839–1914) in uniform with Karl von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. He was elected Prince of Romania on the recommendation of Napoleon III in 1866. In 1881, after achieving formal independence from the Ottoman Empire, Carol declared himself King of Romania.

171ffd50-c8dd-51b6-8ca7-e79ffd9de227.short_description: The rise of tourism saw the production of clothes and items suitable for varying climactic conditions, physical activity, and even potential dangers. This poster foregrounds an image of a hiker in an alpine setting, framed by depictions of many other types of tourism, such as seaside resorts and other more adventurous activities.

17887320-c89a-503d-8231-40a84fa14975.name: *Revolution of 1830 (29 July). Building barricades.*
17887320-c89a-503d-8231-40a84fa14975.short_description: The revolutions of the first half of the 19th century are strongly associated with barricades, usually a pile up of furniture and other objects across streets, aimed at slowing down army troops. There were almost 4,000 barricades in Paris during the revolution of 1830.

179f9d9d-6b5a-52fc-8dea-c159da198fd5.name: *La Reine de Saba: 14 costume sketches*
179f9d9d-6b5a-52fc-8dea-c159da198fd5.short_description: Charles Gounod turned to the librettists Jules Barbier and Michel Carré for advice when he was writing his great opera, and so they recommended him the legend of Hiram, the great tale narrated by Gérard de Nervale in his *Voyage en Orient*. The opera was put on in Paris in 1862. As this costume from the court of Suleiman shows, the models and costumes responded above all to the Orientalist stereotypes in vogue at the time.

17e0e95e-14d7-5aeb-b21f-b18091757a69.name: *Mr. Byzantoine et son ex-libris*, by the Greek cartonist Kem
17e0e95e-14d7-5aeb-b21f-b18091757a69.short_description: Antonis Benakis in Byzantine dress holds his ex-libris and golf clubs, with his dog Mangas and his boat at his feet; on the right, the Russian painter I. Bilibin, below, K. Synadinos, and, top left, ceramics glued together, probably from sherds. Kem’s drawing is a satire on the artistic and athletic interests of Benaki, in the style of Bilibin’s illustrations to Russian legends, for example *The Tale of the Tzar Saltan* (1905).
17e0e95e-14d7-5aeb-b21f-b18091757a69.author: Mina Moraitou

17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.name: *Firework Display Held in Brno on the Occasion of the Coronation of a Picture of the Virgin Mary of St. Thomas*
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.description:
In the 1730s Moravia hosted two festive events offsetting the largest religious festivals of the Czech baroque, the beatification and canonisation of St. John of Nepomuk in Prague (1729). As the capital of the Czech kingdom came into the spotlight for the whole country, so the celebrations of the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns in the Moravian margraviate. These occasions made the Holy Virgin the Queen of Moravia and the patron saint of the country. The festivities around the coronation of the picture of the Virgin Mary in Brno lasted a week. “The night turned into day and the town of Brno into a new heavenly Jerusalem full of scenes of adoration, praise and exultation”. The town's splendour was illuminated by 5,000 lights and plentiful firework displays. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with sculpted decoration and pyrotechnical effects. A detailed programme was issued to accompany the fireworks, explaining the display to viewers in 27 steps.  
After a fanfare of trumpets and tympani, the fireworks were set off by the firing of cannons, and an angel setting white and red fire to the chronogram “Mary the Gem and Patron Saint of the Town of Brno”. Rockets lit up six life-size figures: Emperor Charles IV, who donated the picture, his brother Jan Jindřich, founder of the Augustinian monastery, Pope Clement XII, protector of the adoration picture, the Bishop of Olomouc, who crowned the picture, the prior of the monastery, and the *genius loci* of Brno. The spectacle climaxed with Catherine Wheels at the tips of pyramids and six hearts burning under the figures. The fountain in the foreground started to spew a multitude of tiny stars and blue flowers, while the fire illuminated a flood of garlands. The final highlight of the show, to an overture of cannon fire, was the flight of a two-headed imperial eagle rising with an inscription within mighty flames.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.short_description: Celebrations for the coronation of Marian pictures symbolically confirmed the importance of Olomouc and Brno, the two main towns of the Moravian margraviate. The Holy Virgin became Queen and patron saint of Moravia. The print shows one of the ephemeral festive structures with pyrotechnical effects.

Baran was the artist and engraver of the fireworks print. František Antonín Mayer, a student of Jan Jiří Guttwein, was a bookbinder and engraver in Brno. He executed the engraving of the “silver altar” and the picture of the Brno Thaumaturga.
17f9a63f-8638-5603-ac11-f8d674b5657b.obtention: Purchased in 1978 from an art shop in Brno.

1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.name: *Procession and* Auto de Fé
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.description:
The Inquisition was established during the Verona Council of 1183 for the purposes of the judgment of heresy by the Roman Catholic Church. Necessitated by the emergence of various religious movements and the popularisation of different interpretations of Christian doctrine in opposition to the Roman Church, it was initially called the Episcopal Inquisition because it was administrated by the bishops. Later, in 1230, the Church tried to reform the role and actions of the Inquisition by recruiting professionals mainly from the Dominican Order.  
The new inquisitors judged heresy using local authorities under the Inquisition's procedures. In 1542, three years before the Council of Trent, Pope Paul III established a system of Courts as demanded by the "Supreme Sacred Congregation of the Roman and Universal Inquisition". The Inquisition was established in 1536 in Portugal following a request from King João III.  
Following judgment, defendants were submitted to punishment; a ritual of public penance of condemned heretics and apostates, the so called *Auto de Fé*. In these engravings two important moments of this theatrical religious scene are observed: the Procession taking place in Ribeira Square in Lisbon – close to the Royal Palace of King João V – and the condemned being burned alive at the stake wearing *sambenitos*, clothing with a red cross.  
The Portuguese Inquisition expanded to the colonies: Brazil, Cape Verde and Goa, where it continued as an activity of the religious courts until 1812. In Goa, the processes mostly concentrated on Jews, the Hindu communities and Indian Muslims. The violence of the Inquisition in Goa was so intense that Voltaire wrote: "Goa is sadly famous for its Inquisition, which is contrary to humanity as much as to commerce. The Portuguese monks deluded us into believing that the Indians were worshipping the Devil, while it was them who served him."
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.short_description: The theme of these engravings is related to the brutality of the Inquisition. The Inquisition acted against those whom it deemed heretical and apostates. First they were humiliated and walked through the city in Procession. Then a mass would was said where the sermon preached the morality of the ceremony. Finally they were punished in public in the square.
1811cbd4-6fab-5304-b983-fcad1cbe7fa9.method_for_datation: The engraving is published in the *Annales d'Espagne et de Portugal, contenant tout ce qui s'est passé de plus important dans ces deux royaumes & dans les autres Parties de l'Europe, de même que dans les Indes Orientales & Occidentales, depuis l'établissement de ces deux Monarchies jusqu'á présent. 18197caa-f988-5826-9a1d-d30e87a0bed4.name: Ottoman map of the period of Sultan Abdülhamid II
18197caa-f988-5826-9a1d-d30e87a0bed4.short_description: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. Abdülhamid II was the 34th Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and the last Sultan to exert effective autocratic control over the fracturing state. He oversaw a period of decline in the power and extent of the empire, including widespread pogroms and government massacres against the minorities of the empire (named the Hamidian massacres, after him) as well as an assassination attempt. He ruled from 31 August 1876 until he was deposed shortly after the 1908 Young Turk Revolution, on 27 April 1909.
18197caa-f988-5826-9a1d-d30e87a0bed4.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

183b1889-44b1-5781-a76f-71957bab4067.name: Muhammad ‘Ali Pasha (1769–1849)
183b1889-44b1-5781-a76f-71957bab4067.short_description: Portrait of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha. Although born in Greece, he was the founder of modern Egypt. From Albanian origin, he came to Egypt as an Ottoman officer and began the modernisation of the Egyptian state.

18fa1217-5885-554f-bf5c-aed5d4898cb0.name: Editorial. Inauguration of the Musée Gallo-Romain at the Château de Saint-Germain
18fa1217-5885-554f-bf5c-aed5d4898cb0.short_description: In March 1862, Emperor Napoléon III ordered the "creation of a museum for Celtic and Gallo-Roman antiquities at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye". The castle was restored by Eugène Millet, student of Viollet-le-Duc, who chose to restore it to its condition under François I. A team of confirmed archaeologists were tasked with the organisation of the Museum. Napoléon III wanted a museum dedicated to the archaeology of the national lands (contrary to the collections at the Louvre), and methodically classified: the first curator, Alexandre Bertrand, introduced a chronological classification, breaking the tradition of thematically classified collections. The emperor chose to inaugurate the museum with a symbolically extravagant ceremony, while in Paris the Exposition Universelle (world fair) was in full swing (May 1867).
keywords: Gallo-roman antiquities; Musée de Sain-Germain en Laye

1947528b-a97f-56af-b6c4-fe8372c9bdd5.name: *The Western Wall*
1947528b-a97f-56af-b6c4-fe8372c9bdd5.short_description: The Western Wall of the Haram es-Sharif in Jerusalem, as depicted for the readers of the Illustrated London News by William ‘Crimea’ Simpson. Simpson’s sketches were turned into engravings for publication in the ILN, and were among the most important graphic depictions which helped to introduce western readers to the present-day appearance of Jerusalem and Jerusalemites.

1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.name: The Serious Unemployment Crisis in the Province of Ferrara [central Italy]: Women Preventing the Cavalry from Advancing against the Rioters
1961e839-9c16-5779-a767-870149fec738.short_description:
Violent clashes in the province of Ferrara (Emilia Romagna, Italy) between people who protested against unemployment and the army. The women are in the front line, protecting their comrades from the attacks of the cavalry.  
In 1913, an economic crisis hit Italy. Unemployment grew considerably and so did emigration. In 1913, Italian migration abroad reached its peak: 870.000 Italians migrate abroad. Social tensions and conflicts ran high.

19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.name: *A British Ship Coral Fishing Near Algiers*
19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.short_description: Coral fishing was an important economic activity in the Mediterranean. Algeria was the main fishing area for corals, especially after the depletion of Sardinian coral, and ships from different countries competed for this valuable resource. Torre del Greco, near Naples, was the most important port town for coral fishing in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, while Livorno was the most important port town for coral fishing in the Grand Duke of Tuscany. In 1864, Torre del Greco had 300 coral-fishing boats while Livorno had 60.

1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.name: *View in the Plain of Latakia, in Syria*
1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.short_description: This print, entitled 'View in the Plain of Latakia, Syria' was first published on page 28 of in Robert Brown''s 'The Countries of the World', published by Cassell and Company Ltd, London and New York in 1876. In the 19th century, Latakia was famous for its tobacco, grown in the plain behind the town and on the Ansarieh hills. Three main varieties of tobacco were produced: the lowest quality was dark in colour and strong in flavour; the best, grown in the districts of Diryus and Amamareh, was light and aromatic, exported mainly to Alexandria, Constantinople, Cyprus and directly to Europe.

1b553eb5-5ca4-5f1a-9027-ff3e00f54fe1.name: *Voyage de la Haute Egypte*
1b553eb5-5ca4-5f1a-9027-ff3e00f54fe1.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

1bb390d7-8753-553f-9174-6119a0f96ab1.name: *Exposition Universelle - Their Royal Imperial Majesties and the Viceroy of Egypt visit the Temple of Edfu*
1bb390d7-8753-553f-9174-6119a0f96ab1.short_description: Visitors to the 1867 Exposition Universelle (world fair) had the opportunity to explore a reconstruction of the Temple of Edfu in a "Parc Égyptien". This reconstruction (containing a mix of various different temples) was a response both to the fashion for ancient Egypt, and the desire for good diplomatic relations with modern Egypt. Indeed, we can see the imperial couple in this photograph standing with Isma'il Pasha, the viceroy of Egypt, who had come to see the exhibition. The Temple of Edfu had just been rediscovered by the famous Egyptologist Mariette.
1bb390d7-8753-553f-9174-6119a0f96ab1.artist: Artist: Filippo Liardo; illustrator: Gustave Janet
keywords: Archaeological excavations; Egyptomania; Egypt; World fairs

1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.name: Project for a steamship for the Sultan of Morocco, by the Fratelli Orlando shipyards (Livorno, Italy)
1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.short_description:
Project drawn to a scale 1:100.  
In 1899, the Fratelli Orlando shipyards (Livorno, Italy) made a project of a screw steamer for the Sultan of Morocco. The steamer was to have two decks, two steam engines of 900 HP and harbour twelve passengers. The project, however, was never realised.  
The Fratelli Orlando shipyards built the cruiser Bascir for the Moroccan Navy and a yacht for the Khédivé of Egypt.
1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.author: Daniela Tazzi

1d9fdf68-a63f-5cd6-937f-9223edee8336.name: *Hebron*
1d9fdf68-a63f-5cd6-937f-9223edee8336.short_description: This print is based on a watercolour by David Roberts entitled 'Hebron Mosque erected over the graves of Abraham and the Patriarchs' and completed in 1835. Apparently, this in turn was based on an initial sketch made at the Mosque by a Mrs Bracebridge. According to Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition, the sanctuary at Hebron houses the graves of Abraham, his wife Sarah and their family. To Jews, it is the second holiest site after Jerusalem. Muslims revere the site because of its associations with Abraham and view the city of Hebron as one of the sacred cities of Islam. Formerly prosperous as a glass-manufacturing centre and hajj staging post, Hebron's fortunes declined in the 19th century due to cheap glass imports and the rerouting of the hajj caravan from Damascus to Transjordan.

1e12d773-b67f-5c74-86a0-52e25a1cd507.name: *Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial*
1e12d773-b67f-5c74-86a0-52e25a1cd507.short_description: Joseph Elzéar Morénas (1776–1830) was born to a wealthy family of merchants. Following an early trip to India, Morénas became specialised in botany and developed a love of languages, which even led him to write a Hindi dictionary. When he was sent to Senegal in 1818 he was horrified by what he saw of the slave trade, and so asked to be repatriated. After a sojourn in Haiti, he began working on research in the agricultural sciences, all the while denouncing the "slave trade". His two petitions, "*Pétition contre la traite des noirs*" (1820 and 1821), which he presented to the Chamber of Deputies, created many problems for him. He therefore began working on a *Précis Historique de la Traite des Noirs et de l'Esclavage Colonial* instead, which was published in 1828. He died in Russia, where the Tsar encouraged the continuation of his agronomical work. This title page points to his relationship with and support for Cyril Bissette, a Martinician accused of having written De la Situation des Gens de Couleur Libres aux Antilles Françaises, who was banished by the royal court along with his so-called accomplices (Fabien and Volny).

1ef87e38-e142-56b3-951f-b7d338ff850e.name: *Austrian troops occupy Venice in 1797*
1ef87e38-e142-56b3-951f-b7d338ff850e.short_description: Napoleon ended the existence of the 1000-year-old Venetian Republic in May 1797. French troops proceeded to occupy Venice for six months from May 1797 to January 1798, then ceded the city to Austria. Austrian troops occupied Venice starting 18 January 1798 until the Peace of Pressburg in 1805.

1f2e44d5-854a-519d-868a-777ceb2535e3.name: *Les Folies Turques: quadrille*
1f2e44d5-854a-519d-868a-777ceb2535e3.short_description: The 18th century fascination with "turkeries" was followed in the 19th century by a trend for music with more stereotypical, supposedly "oriental" motifs. This operetta about "turkish follies", is an example of this.

1f36adb3-13ae-550d-b5bc-5e1b31f12bb9.name: Seven plates from *Antiquities and views in Greece and Egypt, with the manners and customs of the inhabitants, from drawings made on the spot*, A.D. 1749 by Richard Dalton
1f36adb3-13ae-550d-b5bc-5e1b31f12bb9.short_description: Between 1746 and 1754, Lord Charlemont, James Caulfield, 1st Earl of Charlemont embarked on a Grand Tour of Europe. Whilst in Sicily in 1749, Charlemont encountered Richard Dalton, a draftsman and engraver, whom he asked to accompany him and his travelling companions onwards to Greece and Egypt in order to provide illustrations for his essays. Dalton travelled with Charlemont until 1750 during which time he made many drawings of landscapes, customs and events and was known as the first Englishman to make drawings in these regions. Some of these drawings were published in ‘*Antiquities and views in Greece and Egypt*’, which was published definitively in 1791 and included engraved sketches of important sites beyond Italy. Notably Dalton also seems to have taken great interest in the annual Hajj procession, and sketched eight different parts of the ceremonies (it is said while concealed in a nearby house), each labelled with an extensive caption. Dalton went on to become librarian to King George III.

1fc5fe5c-fbfa-5316-9126-a887d85076f6.name: *Description de l'Arménie la Perse*
1fc5fe5c-fbfa-5316-9126-a887d85076f6.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Félix Marie Charles Texier was a French historian, architect and archaeologist. Texier published a number of significant works involving personal travels throughout Asia Minor and the Middle East. These books included descriptions and maps of ancient sites, reports of regional geography and geology and descriptions of artwork and architecture.

2014af0a-f0bc-59a2-9a32-22eb77035668.name: Ferdinand I, Czar of Bulgaria (1861–1948)
2014af0a-f0bc-59a2-9a32-22eb77035668.short_description: Portrait of Ferdinand I (1861–1948) as Duke of Bulgaria. In 1908 he made himself Tsar of Bulgaria. Because he joined the German and Austrian monarchy in WWI and lost the war, he had to abdicate on 3 October 1918 and to emigrate to Germany and Slovakia. In 1948 Ferdinand I of Bulgaria died in Coburg, Germany.

20742252-5d4f-565f-8b1e-0849b9510ddd.name: Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861)
20742252-5d4f-565f-8b1e-0849b9510ddd.short_description: Portrait of Abdul-Mejid I, Sultan of Turkey (1823–1861). When he came to power in 1839, he tried to re-occupy lands lost to Muhammad 'Ali, the ruler of Egypt. In this effort he was supported by Britain and Austria. In 1840 a combined British-Austrian fleet cut off the supply lines of the Egyptian army and forced the Egyptians to sign the 1840 Convention of Alexandria. Abdul-Mejid was able to win back Syria and Palestine. In 1849 he granted the Hungarian refugees exile. In 1861 he died and left his throne to his brother Abdülaziz.

2088a0e4-bb93-514d-9d8c-6b0a1e09ef8a.name: *The Necropolis, Petra, March 9th, 1839*
2088a0e4-bb93-514d-9d8c-6b0a1e09ef8a.short_description: The Necropolis' of Petra appears in Volume 3 of 'The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt and Nubia' from drawings made on the spot by David Roberts, lithographed by Louis Haghe and published in six volumes by F.G. Moon in London between 1842-1845. Situated at the beginning of the steep ravine or siq that leads into the heart of Petra, both the so-called 'obelisk tomb' shown in the centre and the Triclinium situated to its lower right still exist today, even if much eroded since the days Roberts visited Petra in 1839. In the 19th century, Petra was one of Europe's most enduring Orientalist fascinations, but it also played a part in the region's more modern history. In October 1917, T. E. Lawrence, to divert Turkish military resources away from the British advance before the Third Battle of Gaza, led a small force of Syrians and Arabs in successfully defending Petra against a combined force of Turks and Germans. Bedouin women from the Petra area - under the leadership of their Sheikh's wife - were recruited to fight in the defense of the city.

21983581-bf0c-5102-8ca7-8f1af359caf4.name: Muhammad Tawfiq Pasha (1852–1892)
21983581-bf0c-5102-8ca7-8f1af359caf4.short_description: Portrait of Muhammad Tawfiq Pasha (1852–1892). 21ba2a39-e5d5-58c6-a42b-e97edf24cfc5.name: Gold medal awarded to l'École Emile-Loubet
21ba2a39-e5d5-58c6-a42b-e97edf24cfc5.short_description: This certificate for a gold medal was awarded to the vocational college l'École Emile-Loubet in Tunis at the Paris International Trade Fair in 1900 for the training it provided particularly in carpentry, metalwork and book binding. 21cf7fa5-ac97-5097-8b52-ba4324bd02bd.name: Edward Dodwell, *View in Greece* (London 1830)
21cf7fa5-ac97-5097-8b52-ba4324bd02bd.short_description: Edward Dodwell recorded the trasformation of the ancient Tower of the Winds into a dervish teke and in the early 19th century it wqas particularly popular with the travellers. Scenes from the city of Athens. Over the lintel, which faces the north-east, upon a red ground, is inscribed the Arabic *La Illah, Allah, Mahamed u resoul ullah* declaring there to be no God but God, and Muhammad to be his prophet. The wooden floor of the interior rests upon the lower cornice, many feet above the ancient pavement. The marble walls are washed with a uniform white. The *mihrab*, painted in perpendicular stripes of green and red, indicates by its position the direction of the Kaaba, or oratory of Mecca; each side of this is a wax candle, and the green flag of the prophet has also its place. The Qur'an is deposited within this niche, and an imitation of the two-edged sword of 'Ali is attached to the adjoining wall. Before these is performed the circularly whirling dance of the Dervishes, witnessing which, the spectator will find it as difficult to remain serious, as it would be dangerous to appear otherwise.

221db0e4-52d5-54d3-a7f0-9a52cbd932ad.name: Italian postcard of colonial propaganda: "Dawn of civilization"
221db0e4-52d5-54d3-a7f0-9a52cbd932ad.short_description: This postcard explicitly states a key element of colonial propaganda: the notion that the colonisers brought “civilisation” to the newly conquered territories. Italian navy ships in the background are intended to convey the notion of Italy’s military might, but nothing reminds viewers of the violence of the colonial enterprise: the military man in the forefront does not carry weapons, but only the Italian flag.

22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.name: The biweekly paper *Spettatore Egiziano* was the first Italian-language newspaper to be published in Egypt
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.short_description:
The *Spettatore Egiziano* was founded in 1845 by Giacomo Castelnuovo, a Jewish medical doctor from Livorno (Tuscany, Italy) who had to flee his country in 1843 because of his affiliation to the Giovane Italia (the Italian patriotic and republican movement created by Giuseppe Mazzini). The *Spettatore Egiziano* was the first Italian-language newspaper to be published in Egypt. Castelnuovo also founded the *Il Progresso d’Egitto*, a bulletin that kept the Italian community in Egypt updated about the Italian political events like the 1848 revolutions.  
Castelnuovo later moved to Tunis where he became the Bey's physician.
22e62379-2fd3-551c-8a81-3883d3d21495.author: Massimo Sanacore

235e2dec-25cb-5d30-8fea-a6de9c3f6d26.name: *The Attack on the Fort of Luft, November 27, 1809*
235e2dec-25cb-5d30-8fea-a6de9c3f6d26.short_description: This depiction shows the fortress of Luft, one of the Qawasim strongholds on the island of Qishm in the Gulf, being attacked by British forces armed with long muskets. Several large dhows are burning in the foreground, while the smoke from defending gunfire can be seen emanating from the loopholes of the fortress. Local fighters are seen lined up along the top the fortress walls and towers.  After having sacked Ras al Khaimah on the Arabian side of the Gulf, the British proceeded to rout out all remaining Qawasim strongholds on the Persian coast, including those on Qishm island. On the 26th of November 1809, the British reached Luft, and after futile negotiations with the local Qawasim representative, they attacked by sea and land. Despite brave and consistent defence which led to heavy British casualties, the fort was taken, all dhows destroyed and the resident Sheikkh exiled.

23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.name: A petition to collect signatures in support of an appeal to the Italian parliament to grant women the right to vote, drawn up by Anna Maria Mozzoni
23c0eaa7-284e-5a97-9ac8-8edafc208719.short_description:
With this appeal, Anna Maria Mozzoni and other women asked members of parliament to leave aside “academic digressions” on women’s nature and on their “mission” and to “consider we \[women\] only in our relation to the State, for what we really are: citizens, taxpayers, and able” who deserved the right to vote.  
Italian women’s campaign to get the right to vote gained momentum at the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th but it wasn’t successful until 1946.  
Anna Maria Mozzoni was the most brilliant Italian feminist activist of the second half of the 19th century. She authored books, founded journals and associations, and incessantly campaigned in favour of women’s rights.

23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.name: Pilgrimage proxy scroll.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.description:
This pilgrimage proxy scroll includes handwriting, painting, and drawing on an expensive yellow glazed paper known as *abadi*. It is in fragmentary condition and its title, as well as the section containing the *basmala* (the formula 'In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful'), are missing. The first of the two fragments includes a pair of standards bearing the name of the contemporary Abbasid caliph, al-Nasir (r. AH 575–622 / AD 1180–1225); the standard on the right is partially preserved. Below this emblem is a colour depiction of Mount Arafat flanked by candlesticks. Below this are depictions of the Maqam-i Ibrahim, a stone associated with the Prophet Abraham, and the water wells. Further below this is a depiction of al-Muzdalifa, where pilgrims spend the night as part of their pilgrimage duties, and al-Mina, which is the third most important site for pilgrims. The empty spaces in between the drawings are filled with inscriptions describing the requirements for the pilgrimage.  
  
The depiction of the Ka'ba unfortunately has not survived in this scroll. The second fragment features depictions of al-Safa and al-Marwa (two locations that pilgrims visit in Mecca), the city of Medina (where pilgrims visit the tomb of the Prophet Muhammad), the city of Jerusalem, which pilgrims customarily visit after the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina, and al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. This proxy certificate was prepared for a person identified as Umm Abbas, wife of Ghalib. The person performing the pilgrimage on her behalf is Ahmad ibn Fadl al-Andalusi. The document was prepared in AH 602 / AD 1206.  
  
In the Middle Ages it was difficult for people, especially women, to go on pilgrimage. Therefore, people who went on pilgrimage themselves, and those who sent a proxy on their own behalves, wanted to own a certificate proving that they had visited the holy sites and fulfilled all the requirements for the pilgrimage (perhaps in order to leave them to the future generations). Such pilgrimage and proxy certificates are invaluable documents for they describe the pilgrimage ritual, depict the holy sites, and provide information regarding the social life of the period.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.short_description: Pilgrimage certificates document pilgrimages to the Holy Lands, culminating in circumambulation of the Ka'ba. The certificates or proxy certificates (for those unable to make the hazardous journey themselves) give the names of the pilgrim and the proxy, the places visited and worship performed, accompanied by pictures.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.obtention: Ismet Bey, the mayor of Istanbul and a member of the board of directors of the Museum of Islamic Foundations (the old name for the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts), visited the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus while travelling. He had a number of items in the Qubbat al-Hazine (Treasury) of the mosque, including Qur'ans and this pilgrimage document, transferred to the Museum where they were registered in the inventory in around 1332 / 1914.

2457b927-f975-5a7e-ab6c-6f0fce7979b6.name: A sheet of a Persian poem
2457b927-f975-5a7e-ab6c-6f0fce7979b6.short_description:
The calligraphy is a Persian poem in three stanzas of two lines by the poet Bidel (1642–1720) who lived in India. Mirza Abdul Qadir Bedil (or Bidel), also known as Bidel Dehlawi, was one of the most influential and successful poets who lived outside Iranian territory and wrote in Persian.  
The poem is written in *taliq* script using iridescent ink. Each stanza is contained in its own cloud-shaped area of white which contrasts the gilt paper background. The edges of the paper are framed by a blue border painted with a scrolling leaf pattern.  
The translation of the poem is as follows:  
“Each man who confides his grief in Him (God, the Beloved) saddens Him / I have a grief which, when I reveal it, causes Him great distress / Sometimes He makes a place in my soul for love and tenderness / sometimes because of the hearts of the others (breaking the hearts of the others) I sadden Him / If I, the heartless (someone who has gone through lots of love grieves in life) reveal my severance (grief of love) to Him, the radiant sun of love for His help /saddens Him greatly."
2457b927-f975-5a7e-ab6c-6f0fce7979b6.method_for_provenance: Purchased from Dr. Friedrich Spuhler, Berlin.

248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.name: The Committee of Tunis for Milan Exhibition 1906
248b6ee3-8b98-5fe8-a126-461e9a621403.short_description: The Italian community in Tunisia participated in the 1906 Milan international exhibition. The Committee in charge of organizing exhibition participation included Italian professionals and entrepreneurs who had migrated from Italy to Tunisia or who were children or grandchildren of immigrants, such as Alfredo Coen (owner of the furniture shop “Au Palais Arabe” and of a furniture factory), G. Di Vittorio and L. Rey (owners of constructions companies that built important public and private buildings, Di Vittorio, from Sicily, Rey, the child of an immigrant from Piedmont), Ugo Moreno (a trader, whose the family had migrated from Livorno in 1830) and Doctor Pietro Brignone (who ran a pharmacy in Tunis).

24a1ef30-391f-5de1-b0c3-ac5c96034a3d.name: Sketch
24a1ef30-391f-5de1-b0c3-ac5c96034a3d.description:
Sketch for a rectangular stained-glass window, comprised of three panels – the outer two narrow and the middle wider. Likely due to this symmetry in design, only the left half of the sketch was completed; thus, the right-hand panel and right half of the middle panel appear empty. The decoration consists of an outer border and rocaille detail in the corners and centre of the design. The centrally positioned main panel features a coat of arms bearing the image of a building. Surrounding this blazon is a medallion with a circular inscription reading “Banco Hispano de Edificación Madrid” (Spanish Bank of Construction, Madrid). The medallion is adorned with a wreath (perhaps of laurel and oak) and construction tools; culminating in a central rosette; surrounded by a frame of trimmed leather and crowned with a scallop shell.  
  
As its inscription indicates, the sketch was made for a stained-glass window to be placed in the Banco Hispano de Edificación. The building that originally housed the bank exists to this day, at 60 Calle Gran Villa in Madrid. The bottom of the sketch bears the workshop registry number and scale of the drawing. As Paloma Pastor notes, in stained-glass window production, the sketch serves as the proposed design. Traditionally, it was offered to the client as a model before carrying out the work. Colour, applied with ink and watercolour pigment, is a fundamental element of these sketches.  
  
Casa Maumejean was a French family business with several branches in Spain, the most renowned of these being the Madrid office. While the company created works for export to diverse locations, the bulk of its production occurred on national soil. Many early-century buildings in Madrid continue to preserve the magnificent stained-glass windows made by the Maumejean company.

251b2b7e-e8f3-5697-9d6d-a33a6facc5ca.name: *Details and ornaments from the Alhambra by Owen Jones, Architect*
251b2b7e-e8f3-5697-9d6d-a33a6facc5ca.description: The influence of the Islamic art also arrived through different publications as the well-known Owen Jones's books and the pieces displayed in the International Exhibitions, as in the first one in London where Owen Jones displayed the Lion fountain of the Alhambra Palace in a building dedicated to master works of art. 261e731d-c1f3-5549-9d76-8e6eb76876e3.name: Alexander I Obrenovic, King of Serbia (1876–1903)
261e731d-c1f3-5549-9d76-8e6eb76876e3.short_description: Portrait of Alexander I Obrenovic, King of Serbia (1876–1903) as a young man. Between the abdication of his father in 1889 and his proclamation as a king in 1893, his mother Natalija Obrenovic ruled as a regent. Being a close ally of Austria, he became Serbian King in 1893. In 1894 Alexander abolished the liberal constitution of Serbia. In 1900 he married Draga Masin, a former lady-in-waiting of his mother. This marriage was very unpopular and weakened the political position of the king. In 1903 he and his wife were murdered by a group of Serbian officers.

26d5c466-64f0-57e3-823b-ed86f67a2c66.name: A postcard of Italian colonial propaganda
26d5c466-64f0-57e3-823b-ed86f67a2c66.description: The Roman Empire once ruled over the entire coastal area of North Africa. This postcard explicitly links the Italian colonial conquest of Libya in 1911-12 with ancient Roman rule over the same territory. It suggests that the Italian Kingdom was the legitimate heir of the Roman Empire and had an historic right to rule over Libya. Especially during Fascism, Italian colonial propaganda often referred to the Roman Empire in order to legitimize Italian expansionist policy.

2714690e-5a6c-5656-b85e-272d60d6e647.description: Horses and camels were the traditional means of travel for nomadic and semi-nomadic groups in the Hijaz and Levant for generations. While the Hijaz Railway meant to industrialise the pilgrim travel from Damascus to Medina, quadrupeds remained an essential part of the pilgrimage route, as well as vital resources for the construction of the railway itself. While the railway served as a mechanised replacement for their labour, horses and camels remained vital to the path of the railway before, during and after its construction.
