2735c542-1b56-59a7-9fac-72518fe82535.name: Blueprint map of the Hijaz railway line between Damascus and Medina
2735c542-1b56-59a7-9fac-72518fe82535.short_description:
In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line began from Damascus and reached Medina in 1908, never reaching Mecca.  
This map, which is dated 28 Huzayran 1334 (28 June 1916), shows the Hijaz railway line from Damascus to Medina and Dar‘a to Haifa, with a dotted line marking the line between Medina and Mecca (a line which was never completed). Names of stops and tribal territories are marked. The map is signed by the German Heinrich August Meissner – the chief engineer of the Hijaz railway. In 1904 he was given an official title and was known as Meissner Pasha. The original sketches for Hijaz railway maps were made by Mukhtar Bey, an accomplished engineer from Istanbul who was responsible for the original surveys of the route. They were then drawn by other officers and the blue prints signed off by Meissner, perhaps with changes. Mukhtar Bey was known as ‘Meissner’s right hand man’. The date here is notable as the Arab Revolt, which saw sections of the railway destroyed, began in June 1916.

27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.name: *The Ruins of the Temple of the Sun at Baalbec*
27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.short_description: This dramatic view looks across the great court of the temple complex in Baalbek. In the ancient world Baalbek, to the east of Beirut in Lebanon, was a great centre of trade between Europe and Asias, and home to a religion of sun worship. The Scottish artist David Roberts visited in 1839 and over the following years made many images of the still imposing ruins. This painting is Roberts's last of Baalbek, and he considered it as 'a grand finale' to his career as a painter of the Middle East. The complex's imposing architectural and artistic details also inspired European Neoclassical architects and artists such as Robert Adam. Since about 1864 many tourists visited the famed site, including, in 1898, the German emperor Wilhelm II on his way to Jerusalem. Struck by the magnificence of the ruins, he dispatched a German archaeological team, whose subsequent work resulted in a meticulously presented and illustrated publication that further raised interest in Baalbek.

27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.name: *Magnificent Atrium with Figures*
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.description:
The growing influence and interaction between communications, especially the printing press and foreign travel, reinforced the cosmopolitan culture that came to characterise the processes of the European courts. Lisbon took the lead, when, under the reign of the King João V, Absolutism gave the Portuguese monarchy a renewed lease of life. Sacred and profane music, heard either at the Patriarch or at court, had a strong political meaning and reinforced the king's aura of majesty. King João V, therefore, commissioned artists such as Domenico Scarlatti; built the monumental Opera House next to the Royal Palace in 1754 (destroyed during the earthquake of 1755), and enlarged the Royal Orchestra with new foreign soloists.  
The theatrical scenery drawings of the Galli Bibiena family were not made on durable material. Due to the fact that the theatre sets they designed for court functions were temporary, few of their creations have survived. The richness and splendour of their stage sets can however still be judged from contemporary drawings, preserved in great numbers, and found mainly in collections in [Vienna](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), [Munich](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich") and [Dresden](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden "Dresden").  
This drawing by Francesco Galli Bibiena is a study for an unknown stage set. It is possible that it was brought to Portugal in 1750–1751 by his son, Giovanni Carlo Sicino Bibiena (1717–1760), who was charged by King José I to modernise both the theatres themselves and their services.  
The drawing shows an interior space with large arcades seen from a diagonal perspective. The composition is dominated by two large arches leading up to corridors at the top of a staircase. The vaults are richly decorated and the balconies bear several medallions with mythological figures at the centre supported by little angels. Bound by columns and female sculptures, the central area is occupied by women with children. Two dogs can be seen on the left. Through the main arcade a young crowned ruler makes his entrance surrounded by soldiers carrying banners, attracting everyone's attention.
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.short_description: This drawing by Francesco Galli Bibiena is a study for an unknown stage set. It represents an interior space with large arcades seen from a diagonal perspective. The vaults are richly decorated and the balconies bare several medallions with mythological figures at the centre supported by angels.
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.initial_owner: Probably belonged to Giovanni Carlo Sicino Bibiena (1717–1760)
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.method_for_datation: Stylistic approach to the graphical work of Francesco Galli Bibiena.
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.provenance: Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Lisbon, 1884
27db4792-06af-5d09-8d3d-457d76486f2e.obtention: The drawing might have been brought to Portugal by Giovanni Carlo Sicino Bibiena in 1751 or 1752, along with some others. There is little information about the whereabouts of these drawings during the second half of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th. In around 1845 the drawing was in the collection of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, Lisbon and then transferred to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in 1884, the date of its establishment.

This poster, for examples, claims that a simple credit system would allow this family to radically change their life, affording them a larger and better lit home, nicer clothes, and a more luxurious dinner on the table.

28ec76df-2d4c-59e5-8b93-2cd4db3c1960.name: Labour certificate No.1(a) [Child’s labour certificate]
28ec76df-2d4c-59e5-8b93-2cd4db3c1960.short_description: Under the Employment of Children Act 1903, a child needed to obtain such a certificate (by passing a certain grade standard in school work) before being able to leave school and commence employment. The certificate is divided into two parallel sections, both stamped with the signature of James Graham, a Local Education Authority officer. The left-hand one gives the holder's name (Annie Waggonheim), address and birthdate, and certifies that she is not less than thirteen years old according to her birth certificate or statutory declaration. The right-hand section certifies that she has made 350 attendances in not more than two schools during each year for five preceding years, and gives 'Darley St C School' (Darley Street Council School) as the school in which the attendances were made.

28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.name: North African caravan, in the west of the Sahara
28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.short_description: Camille Douls (1864–1889), who was passionate  about Africa, decided in the late 19th century to enter indigenous North African territory, despite it being forbidden for foreigners at the time. He began to learn Arabic and study the Quran for this purpose, and was able to live among the Oulad Delim tribe for five months, although not without risk to his personal safety. He published his observations on his return (1888), which attracted much attention, as no European had lived among these people to date. He was assassinated the following year during a trip to Algeria. The tale of his time in the desert was illustrated by Jules Girardet, an artist specialising in historical scenes who had never seen the subjects of his drawings. This image is therefore interesting, as it sheds light on the nature of the stereotypical Western gaze on nomadic lifestyles.

28f9592c-7e7c-553c-be06-baac37d4447b.name: *The arrival of Suleiman Pasha, envoy of the Porte, in Giurgiu*
28f9592c-7e7c-553c-be06-baac37d4447b.short_description: In June 1848 revolution broke out in Wallachia, aiming to liberate the country from the Ottoman sovereignty. Prince Bibescu was deposed and a provisional government was installed. As a result, the sultan sent an army to Wallachia. The Ottoman army entered on the Romanian territory in July and the Porte’s representative, Suleiman Pasha, began negotiations with the Romanian revolutionary government. This chromolithograph is part of a series of German chromolithographs depicting episodes from the Revolution that took place in Wallachia in 1848. It shows the entrance of Süleyman Pasha, the Porte's envoy, accompanied by a part of his army of 20.000 soldiers, in Giurgiu, a port on the Danube, after having crossed the river. He is received by a Romanian delegation.

2bc79611-c941-5b21-81f7-7525e5e187ea.name: An example of Italian colonial propaganda describing 'The first railway engine crossing Libya, causing astonishment and panic among the Arabs'
2bc79611-c941-5b21-81f7-7525e5e187ea.short_description:
The railway in a colonial context was much more than a means of transport: it was a powerful symbol of modernity, of technological superiority of the colonisers over the colonised, and of mastery over the territory. The construction of railways in colonial situations was thus often celebrated by the colonialists’ popular press or in postcards, as in this case.  
In Libya, the Italians started building railroads from the first months of colonial rule. The first lines, inaugurated in 1912, connected Tripoli with Ain Zara (11 kms) and to Zanzur (39 kms). By the end of 1915, the railway lines in Libya amounted to 180 kilometres.
2bc79611-c941-5b21-81f7-7525e5e187ea.author: Giulia Barrera

2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.name: *Turkish Country Houses on the Bosphorus*
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.short_description: This engraving shows the typical, wooden Ottoman yalis or summer houses built along the shores of the Bosphorus by high-ranking officials and members of the elite since the late 17th century. Designed to reflect both their location, making maximum use of the waterfront, and the taste and status of their owner, the yalis provided a welcome and comfortable escape from the congested city. Their interior, with separate areas for public reception and private family quarters, was furnished, with inbuilt cupboards and diwans, and decorated in the traditional Ottoman style. Only in the 19th century were aspects of European-style interior design and furniture adopted widely. The facades of the yalis were traditionally painted a deep rose colour, until European influence led to the adoption of pastel shades in the 19th century. The image was originally published in Julia Pardoe's 'The Beauties of the Bosphorus', published in London by George Virtue in 1838.

2cf5398f-8d6e-5e13-b679-67442f1bcbc6.name: Menu for the gala dinner offered by the Italian king in honour of the Ambassador from Morocco, who visited Italy in June 1890
2cf5398f-8d6e-5e13-b679-67442f1bcbc6.short_description:
In June 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent an Ambassador to Italy (Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi), to meet the Italian King and present him with extremely rich gifts.  
The Ambassador – who was escorted by his secretary, an interpreter, and some dignitaries – was received with the highest honours. He met with the Italian Prime Minister and with the King, who offered a gala dinner for him.  
The menu for the gala dinner was in French. A military band played different pieces of music during the dinner.

2ea7c030-0b7a-51c2-aa26-875093afd861.name: Life-size templates for the curtain of the door of the Ka‘ba
2ea7c030-0b7a-51c2-aa26-875093afd861.short_description:
The majority of the Ka‘ba door curtains made at Dar al-Kiswa during the 19th century follow the same basic design in which calligraphic cartouches predominate and which is characterized by the series of stylized ‘palm trees’ either side of the door opening.  
  
Due to their size, Ka‘ba door curtains were made in four sections which were embroidered separately then joined together. They were known as *al-‘ataba*, *al-tiraz*, *al-qa’im al-saghir* and *al-qa’im al-kabir*, and these actual-size tinted drawings set out the layout and decorative patterns of each. Areas ito be embroidered in silver are tinted blue, whereas those which were to be embroidered in silver-gilt wire are in yellow. The Collection also includes life-size templates for the curtains of the internal door of the Ka‘ba; for the Meccan *minbar*; for the *kiswa* of Maqam Ibrahim; and for the door of the Maqsurat Ibrahim, from the same set.

2efb58fe-14fe-59df-ad70-18b84374d4f5.name: Edmund Count Szechenyi (1839–1922)
2efb58fe-14fe-59df-ad70-18b84374d4f5.short_description: Portrait of Count Edmund Szechenyi. He was born in 1839 in Bratislava and studied the work of fire brigades in London. In 1869 he founded in Budapest the first volunteer fire brigade, which was transformed into a professional fire brigade in 1870. From 1871–1874 he commanded the umbrella organisation of all fire brigades in Hungary. In 1875 he was sent by Emperor Franz Joseph to Istanbul to build up a fire brigade in the Ottoman capital. As head of the fire brigade he became the first Christian Pasha in the Ottoman Army and stayed in Istanbul until his death in 1922.

2f387f4d-1ef9-59c3-bf8a-f4bf6e3f9be9.name: *Varaždin Merchant, Joannes Friedrich, in his Shop*
2f387f4d-1ef9-59c3-bf8a-f4bf6e3f9be9.description:
The print shows the cartouche-framed interior of the merchant, Joannes Friedrich’s shop, situated in Tomislav Square in Varaždin. Dressed in the Rococo fashion with a powdered wig, he is sitting at a desk holding a quill pen in one hand and a letter in the other. In front of him stands a customer in a long coat. Two Rococo windows and a row of shelves for merchandise and accounting books are in the background. A cartouche at the bottom of the picture reads “BARONE IOANNE DI FRIDRICO SENATORE ET MERCATORE DI VARASDINO”. (Baron Joannes Friedrich Senator and Merchant of Varaždin).  
Quite a few members of the nobility were merchants who invested in the economy, an aspect that marks the beginning of capitalism and mass production.
2f387f4d-1ef9-59c3-bf8a-f4bf6e3f9be9.short_description: The print shows the cartouche-framed interior of the merchant, Joannes Friedrich’s shop, situated in Tomislav Square in Varaždin. Friedrich, portrayed serving a customer, was also Senator of the Varaždin Town Council.

2fd7dbb0-f684-52f4-93f3-b485ecf82f5e.description: This curious postcard with a utopian vision of how the Strait of Gibraltar could become in the future was sent to the Marquis of Cerralbo by a friend, Gabriel Vich, but never received a stamp. Although it shows the address of the marquis, maybe it was posted inside an envelope or delivered, finally, on hand. This kind of ephemera was published by the fortnightly publication España en África (Spain in Africa), active in the first decades of the 20th century. The image represented is a beautiful commercial and geopolitical project that would have linked two continents with a 15 km bridge.

31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.name: Statue of Cardinal Lavigerie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.short_description: On the 23 November 1925, the French resident-general in Tunisia, Lucien Saint, organised a solemn gathering to commemorate 100 years since Cardinal Lavigerie's birth. The municipality of Tunis also received a statue of him brandishing a cross by the sculptor Élie-Jean Vézien, which they chose to put in Place Bab el-Bhar (at the entrance to the medina), a place of great importance to Tunisians. This choice of location angered the Tunisian population and triggered a protest from the students of the Zaytuna University, who considered this act an attack on their religious beliefs (it was placed close to the Zaytuna Mosque) and their traditions. The statue stayed there until Tunisian independence, when it was removed by the Mayor of Tunis.  Lavigerie was the Archbishop of Algiers and Carthage, and the founder of the Pères Blancs in 1868.

32533015-dfdb-5437-8c81-e020001b7470.name: *The Suffragette 1d Weekly*
32533015-dfdb-5437-8c81-e020001b7470.short_description:
‘The Suffragette’ was the weekly newspaper of the Woman's Social and Political Union (WSPU), the leading militant organisation campaigning for women’s suffrage in the United Kingdom. This wood block printed advertisement features the patron saint of the Suffragettes, Joan of Arc carrying the banner of the WSPU.  
  
Hilda Dallas was a member of the Suffrage Atelier, which was formed in 1909 to encourage artists to promote 'the enfranchisement of women, by means of pictorial publication'. Its activities also included training non-professional artists in printing techniques. The low cost, low tech method of wood block printing, as used in this poster, was cheap, quick and easy to learn.

32ae501a-15d6-534c-9b3c-572d30f5a223.name: *Allegory of the Prosperity of Moravia under the Beneficent Reign of Leopold I*
32ae501a-15d6-534c-9b3c-572d30f5a223.description:
An allegory of Moravia: a map in the shape of the globe, i.e. the Moravian world, is surrounded by celestial powers, representative of the states (clergy, nobility, towns) and allegorical figures. The woman with a mirror kneeling on the left personifies *Prudentia* (deliberation or foresight), while *Fortitudo* (courage or resolution) is represented by a female figure with a massive column and a Heraclean lion-skin on her head, close to another female figure with an hourglass embodying *Moderatio* (temperance or self-discipline). The symbolically raised hand with the scales over Moravia belongs to *Justitia* (Justice). The dignified man with a wig, with one hand on a *fasces* (a bundle of white birch rods) and the other on a statue of Pallas Athene, may be interpreted as an allegory of *bonum consilium* – good advice – as well as education. The celestial powers testify to the prosperity of the land under Emperor Leopold I (1657–1705), whose monogram *LI* is the centre piece of the print. The fruit of his beneficent reign is indicated by cornucopias, as well as by the attributes of education, and stones with planetary symbols corresponding to silver and iron, the wealth of the country.  
At the centre, the imperial eagle supports a picture of the miraculous Virgin Mary of St. Thomas, accompanied by patron saints Cyril and Methodius on the left and St. Wenceslas on the right. The function of the celestial sphere carried by angels is specified by the words: “Divine power rules the celestial worlds” on a band. The peculiar manner of representation, with Moravia as a globe, is elucidated by the second part of the sentence, at the interface of the heavenly and earthly spheres: “and the emperor rules the Moravian world with fatherly, powerful care”. The print originated as part of an Olomouc University thesis. After taking exams, graduates had to participate in public debates, the theses of which were printed as announcements. Some of them were engraved after templates by Moravian painters in the renowned Augsburg workshops.
32ae501a-15d6-534c-9b3c-572d30f5a223.short_description: The print originated as an Olomouc thesis. Some of these were engraved after templates by Moravian painters in the renowned Augsburg workshops. As well as the principal patron saints of the land, the print presents personifications of good government, considered to be a prerequisite of the country’s prosperity.
32ae501a-15d6-534c-9b3c-572d30f5a223.method_for_datation: The original artist remains unknown. The print is signed by the Olomouc copperplate engraver Antonín Freindt (1664–1727). The print also features the name of the person who commissioned it and whose thesis is seen in the Latin text at the bottom section of the print.
32ae501a-15d6-534c-9b3c-572d30f5a223.obtention: The print was a part of a collection of university theses from Olomouc University, established in 1573 as a Jesuit College. The collection was taken into the state archives in the 1950s.

33430dbe-c0fc-5bb4-9845-6bce853a6ea6.name: General Hullin's audience, provided by the Dey of Algeria
33430dbe-c0fc-5bb4-9845-6bce853a6ea6.short_description: In August 1802, irritated by the repeated pillaging of his ships by Algerian pirates, Napoléon I sent General Hullin and Consul Dubois-Thainville to the then Dey of Algeria, Mustafa Pasha, with a threatening message. This print is an example of Napoleonic propaganda, as it attempts to highlight the "insolence" of the bey, who stays seated on the sofa, and the "bravery" of the general who, with a sword on his side, makes his speech.

340abb76-0aa3-53e7-b9ea-c4ebf5b8737b.name: Pharaoh Rameses II in the act of killing enemies with his spear
340abb76-0aa3-53e7-b9ea-c4ebf5b8737b.short_description: The print reproduces the drawing, today at the University Library of Pisa, realised by Giuseppe Angelelli. Angelelli’s painting is used for Table LXXXIII of the Historical Monuments which shows one of the engraved paintings from the southern wall of the temple of Abu Simbel, celebrating King Ramses piercing his enemy with a spear. This is a traditional scene that has been reproduced on numerous Egyptian monuments from early historic periods to show the supremacy of the Pharaoh above all foreign people. The enemies of the Egyptians are characterised by libic hair and dresses. An error was made by the copier in the spear used by Rameses, possibly reproduced within Angelelli’s painting because of the Director of the Commission wanted to correct the hieroglyphical text above.

341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.name: The port of Brăila
341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.short_description: In 1829, an annex to the peace treaty of Edirne, that was concluded after the Russo-Ottoman war of 1828-1829, concerned the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia. One of its provisions was that the Sublime Porte had to give back to Wallachia the three cities situated on the left bank of the Danube, which it had conquered in the 15h-16th centuries. Among these was Brăila, a port on the Danube annexed by the Ottomans at around 1540. After 1829 measures were taken by the local authorities for the modernization of Brăila. The port subsequently developed thanks to the growth of Wallachian commerce as a consequence of the fact that by the treaty of Edirne the Ottoman Empire granted the freedom of commerce to the Romanian Principalities. In 1838 Brăila was given the status of free port (with no or few customs duties).

3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.name: The female surgery division of the Italian hospital in Tunis
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.short_description:
Prior to the establishment of the French protectorate on Tunisia in 1881, Italian doctors operated in Tunisia. The Bey had frequently employed Italian physicians. Some were born in Tunisia, of Jewish families from Livorno, others had arrived in Tunisia as political exiles in the first half of the 19th century. The largest contingent of Italian doctors, however, migrated to Tunisia after 1881.  
In 1890, the Italian community opened a hospital with about 100 beds. Italian physicians worked in the hospital as volunteers and indigent patients were treated for free. The initial funding for creating and running the hospital came from the Italian community; the Italian state contributed to pay the expenses for the construction of a new facility in 1900 and partly subsidized the hospital activities.
3461e5ef-930c-5a8d-8393-eeb23e8eaffa.author: Giulia Barrera

34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.name: *Portico of the Temple at Edfu, Upper Egypt*
34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.short_description: Considered the best preserved cult temple of ancient Egypt, Edfu temple was swamped with sand in Roberts’s days, and houses had been built on top. The French archaeologist Auguste Mariette eventually excavated it in the 1860s.This view shows the temple's portico, its  sand-filled façade supported by six monumental columns. The columns on either side of the centre have large lotus columns, those flanking them are made to resemble vertically rising date palm fronds. The outermost columns carry capitals derived from composite Theban palm tree designs. Beyond the columns of the facade, two further rows of capitaled columns form the inner area of the portico, or pronaos. Over the entrance of the portico and on the upper shafts of the columns, pharaonic imagery, emblems, cartouches and hieroglyphs are clearly visible.  The artist emphasizes the monumentality of both the portico and the masses of sand that have invaded it by introducing a group of dwarfed visitors resting on one of the sand dunes in the centre – utterly dwarfed by their surroundings.
34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority

35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.name: *The Moroccan Embassy in Rome*
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.short_description:
In June 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent an Ambassador to Italy (Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi), to meet the Italian King and present him with gifts.  
The Ambassador was received with the highest honours. He met with the Italian Prime Minister and with the King, who offered him a gala dinner.  
In these pictures one can see (from the top left): four captains who escorted Morocco’s Ambassador, his interpreter Lamfaddal Elkabbagi, the Ambassador on a carriage arriving at the King’s palace, Hamed (one of the Ambassador’s servants), Pà Nadan (another servant), and two children travelling with the Ambassador on the hotel’s terrace.
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
35118a9c-ae87-5875-b6fd-694c3a29ac01.author: Giulia Barrera

351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.name: Au Palais Arabe. A furniture shop of the Italians Eugenio and Alfredo Coen in Tunis
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.short_description: “Au Palais Arabe”, Rue de Rome, 3, Tunis, was once the most important shop in town for furniture and other household items. Eugenio Coen (born in Livorno in 1855, migrated to Tunis in 1885) and his brother Alfredo (born in Livorno in 1868 and migrated to Tunis in 1887) also ran a furniture factory that, in 1906, employed about 100 carpenters, cabinet makers and other workers, 80 per cent of whom were Italian.
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th–early 20th century
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.author: Giulia Barrera

351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.name: *Mosque of Sidi Bu Madyan, Tlemcen, Algeria*
351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.short_description: The mosque adjoins the shrine of Sidi Bu Madyan, a twelfth century holy-man, and was built by the Marinid dynasty in 1339. Fabrizi's view shows clearly the richly carved stucco decoration framing the simple horseshoe arches; through one of these is seen the tiled mihrab (niche indicating the direction of Mecca) and the wooden minbar (pulpit). Fabrizi has captured the moment after the formal prayers when each worshipper makes a personal supplication to Allah, holding his hands out in a gesture to receive His blessing.
351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.author: Victoria and Albert Museum

3540af77-ea01-5e4b-bd04-3e31d3b139e4.name: Poster for the International Exhibition of Milan, 1906, depicting the opening of the Simplon Tunnel
3540af77-ea01-5e4b-bd04-3e31d3b139e4.short_description: Leopoldo Metlicovitz worked as a lithographer and an illustrator. Among his works are illustrations for the Milanese newspaper *La Sera*, opera librettos and some cover pages of *Corriere della Sera*. He also made posters for an auto exhibition, an insurance company and the opening of the Simplon Tunnel in 1906. The erotic male nude recalls Michelangelo’s figures. The poster was chosen by the Committee of the International Exhibition despite the fact the it was not submitted within the competition. The artist depicts the personification of Progress and Science ideally leading the convoy towards the light beyond the tunnel. The tunnel, almost 20 kilometres long, was started following an 1895 agreement between Italy and Switzerland. The works were finished after long difficulties and the railway was opened on June 1, 1906 and celebrated at the Universal Exposition in Milan.

3549f5be-8ae2-53fd-9501-cb96736906e9.name: Panoramic view of the city of Mecca, painted by Muhammad ‘Abdallah, the Delhi cartographer
3549f5be-8ae2-53fd-9501-cb96736906e9.short_description:
The view of Mecca is remarkable for its comprehensiveness and accuracy and, in the manner of contemporary topographers, brilliantly combines a plan of the city with a bird’s-eye view from about 60 degrees. Muhammad ‘Abdallah, whose grandfather, Mazar ‘Ali Khan was court painter to the Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah II, was commissioned by the Sharif of Mecca to depict the sacred monuments of his realm in the second quarter of the 19th century.  
  
This is the earliest known accurated depiction of the Masjid al-Haram and the immediate vicinity. The painting is also unique among such representations in its inclusion of a ‘vignette’ of a man attending to his jars…
3549f5be-8ae2-53fd-9501-cb96736906e9.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection

355b8a63-ea50-5b91-9873-7e2c8152cab8.name: *Catholic mission to Brazzaville: Brazzaville mission school - Vive la France!*
355b8a63-ea50-5b91-9873-7e2c8152cab8.short_description: Evangelism and colonialism often went hand in hand, working together to Christianise local populations. The missionaries considered French society as the perfect model of Christian society, and the government thought missions would help consolidate colonialism. Schools were one of the places where this relationship is the most evident. This image clearly shows how the French instilled young African children with love for the French flag from a very young age.

35b961a6-875c-5ccf-a80f-d6f917ccd48e.name: Jozef Zachariasz Bem (1795–1850)
35b961a6-875c-5ccf-a80f-d6f917ccd48e.short_description: Portrait of Jozef Zachariasz Bem as Turkish Pasha. Jozef Bem was born in the Austrian part of Poland. He fought as a Napoleonic officer against the Russians. In 1830 he participated in the Polish uprising against the Russians in Warsaw. In 1848 he was one of the leading Generals fighting with the Hungarian army against the Habsburg troops. After several defeats in 1849, he fled with 6,000 Hungarian-Polish soldiers to the Ottoman Empire. After converting to Islam, he became a Turkish General. In 1850 he suppressed an Arabic pogrom against the Christian population of Aleppo.
keywords: Jozef Zachariasz Bem; Aleppo; Syria; Hungary

36e1b6b4-30ae-5caf-b227-73b35b67c02b.name: Fuad I, King of Egypt (1868–1936)
36e1b6b4-30ae-5caf-b227-73b35b67c02b.short_description: Portrait of Fuad I, King of Egypt (1868–1936). In 1917 Fuad I succeeded his brother Hussein Kamil as Sultan of Egypt. In 1922, after Egypt had achieved independence from the Ottoman Empire, he became King of Egypt with the help of the British government.
keywords: Fuad I, King of Egypt; Hussein Kamil

370bd873-8035-59b2-bc6d-9c176b57e9d5.name: Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848)
370bd873-8035-59b2-bc6d-9c176b57e9d5.short_description: Portrait of Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848). As the best General under his father Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, he fought successfully against the Wahhabites, the Ottoman Army and the Greeks. In 1831 he conquered Syria and governed it until 1841. In 1848 he deposed his senile father and was declared Vice King of Egypt by Sultan Abdülmecid I.

3729e16c-4e7e-5f2a-ab2f-106e9ada1d33.name: Postcard
3729e16c-4e7e-5f2a-ab2f-106e9ada1d33.short_description: Postcard; printed paper; photograph showing a view across downtown Zarqa, Jordan.

374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.name: *Tuğra* of Sultan Osman III.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.description:
The Sultan's official monogram or *tuğra* (tughra) is drawn in gold outlined with black ink on a blue ground. The areas between the letters in the lower part of the *tuğra*, the 'arms' of the *tuğra*, and its flaring bow are filled with floral decoration. These floral compositions show two different styles: one following the Chinese influence *hatayi*\-style, and the other reflecting the appearance of baroque designs in Ottoman illumination under European influence. In the upper right-hand corner are depictions of the Ka'ba in Mecca and of Medina rendered in an oval frame. The paintings of Mecca and Medina resemble similar compositions in AH 11th–12th- / AD 17th–18th- century decorative arts, manuscript painting and tiles. In the lower left-hand corner is a medallion containing the signature of the artist who drew the *tuğra*, Karabağlı Kaptan-ı Derya Süleyman Pasha, phrased thus: 'The slave of the court, Süleyman Pasha, made the *tuğra* of the Sultan of the world'. The date AH 1270 (AD 1854) is also given. This is surprising and possibly incorrect for Kaptan-ı Derya (Grand Admiral) Süleyman Pasha does not appear in the historical sources for that year. He was promoted to that rank by Sultan Osman III in AH 1168 / AD 1754 and remained in that position until he was removed from it in AH 1171 / AD 1757. In the same year he was restored to his post by Sultan Mustafa III (r. AH 1171–87 / AD 1757–74) and remained in it until AH 1172 / AD 1759. Since the work has undergone much restoration in various periods, the date must be AH 1170 / AD 1756–7 rather than AH 1270 / 1853–4.  
  
Sultan Osman III, who ascended the throne at age fifty-five, was the oldest Ottoman prince to become sultan, and his reign lasted only three years. The *tuğra* reads 'Osman Khan, son of Mustafa, ever-victorious'. The *tuğra* was a kind of signature of the Ottoman sultans, drawn by a special official of the Imperial Chancery (*Divan-ı Hümayun*) or under his instruction. Because of its size and the fact that it is executed so as to display in detail all the aspects of a *tuğra*, this example must have been made in the Imperial Chancery as a model with the aim of ensuring that *tuğra* copies could be made without any mistakes.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.short_description: *Tughras*, official monograms of the sultans, are one the first things to come to mind when Ottoman art or history is mentioned. The size of this *tughra* of Sultan Osman III makes it an interesting example and it has features peculiar to the art of the AH 12th / AD 18th century.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.method_for_datation: Dated according to the signature, in which the name of the Grand Admiral Süleyman Pasha appears; he was Grand Admiral during the reign of Sultan Osman III. (No other Grand Admiral by that name was found in the historical sources for reigns other than that of Osman III).
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.method_for_provenance: Only the Imperial Chancery (*Divan-ı Hümayun*) was allowed to print the sultan's *tuğra*. Large examples like this one were prepared as models to ensure that the *tuğra* was drawn correctly when added to official documents. Thus, it must have been produced in the Topkapı Palace, Istanbul.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.obtention: Transferred to the Museum in 1916 from the library of Kılıç Ali Paşa in Istanbul.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.bibliography: Ölçer, N., *et al, In Pursuit of Excellence: The Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts*, Istanbul, 1993, p.43, pl. 22, 61.
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.artist: Kaptan-ı Derya (Grand Admiral) Karabağlı Süleyman Pasha, court tuğra artist (dates of service: AH 1168–71 / AD 1754–57).
374a32ae-e579-53c0-bfce-25a5e5c80764.author: Sevgi Kutluay
keywords: Wood; gilding; watercolour; painting; tuğra; tughra

377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.name: Scroll with views of Mecca and Medina
377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.short_description: The text consists of Qur’anic verses, short prayers, invocations and numerous repetitions of the *basmala* and the *shahada*, the latter arranged into decorative shapes such as vases, flowers, a pagoda and *Dhu’l-faqar*, the bifurcated sword given by the Prophet to ‘Ali. In addition, there are depictions of the Masjid al-Haram at Mecca and the Prophet’s mosque at Medina (where the domed tomb is depicted on the wrong side). The last panel encloses the *hilya* of the Prophet Muhammad.

3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.name: Egyptian Furniture of the Italian Giuseppe Parvis Living in Cairo [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.short_description: Giuseppe Parvis, who emigrated from Italy to Egypt, began extensive production of elegant furniture adapted to Arabian taste and decorated with mother-of-pearl and metal inserts. He won awards for his work at the Universal Exhibitions of Paris in 1867, Vienna and Philadelphia. Giuseppe Parvis is an example of successful businessman who successfully adapted to the Egyptian market. He was able to run laboratories with 50 workers and trained a large number of students in ebony furniture making. Over the span of 20 years he introduced and sold furniture to Arabian people who traditionally did not possess such furniture, using an Arabic style and taste and by using woods found in the East, Egypt and China.
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.

390fed84-29b4-5b5f-8552-8a2d440391d6.name: *Colonial Education*
390fed84-29b4-5b5f-8552-8a2d440391d6.short_description: This article on the "colonial education" the youth received in France, published in a newspaper for the French community in Tunisia, has a didactic objective, encouraging and legitimising French economic colonialism in Tunisia, and thus also the migration of French youth to Tunisia.

392f3d7f-32c6-5e59-aeea-0cf54fb842cc.name: *The Victoria Nile - At Rionga's Island*
392f3d7f-32c6-5e59-aeea-0cf54fb842cc.short_description: People had been trying to find the source of the Nile since antiquity. However, interest in this increased significantly in the early 19th century, and lead to various scientific observations. These observations were published and illustrated with engravings, which allowed Europeans to better understand the African continent.

39c5d2fa-be8f-55e6-97ea-9cd4b0e30514.name: *Constantinople et le Bosphore de Thrace*
39c5d2fa-be8f-55e6-97ea-9cd4b0e30514.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

3a20e143-6e36-5c47-8630-b7694a01419b.name: Jubbeh
3a20e143-6e36-5c47-8630-b7694a01419b.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader

3a479e74-ad19-5334-a508-9d331c6ee9bd.name: 'Air force'
3a479e74-ad19-5334-a508-9d331c6ee9bd.short_description: In 1911, in Libya, the newly founded Italian Air Force carried out the very first aerial bombing of civilian targets in world history. Italian anti-colonialists vocally protested such practice, as Scalarini’s cartoon shows.

3a6414c9-05eb-59ee-b5b1-43057ab8b195.name: *Chateaubriand at the ruins of Carthage*
3a6414c9-05eb-59ee-b5b1-43057ab8b195.short_description: This engraving of the French poet René de Chateaubriand shows him sitting on a hill facing the sea, surrounded by the ruins of Carthage. Fascinated by Didon's city and its glorious past, the poet visited Carthage in January 1807, and recorded his observations in his book entitled *Itinéraire de Paris à Jérusalem et de Jérusalem à Paris en Allant par la Grèce, en Revenant par l’Egypte*, published in Paris in 1811 by Lenormant, in three volumes.
3a6414c9-05eb-59ee-b5b1-43057ab8b195.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
3a6414c9-05eb-59ee-b5b1-43057ab8b195.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar

3b3c9b35-91d8-5460-af41-e16d0268e789.name: Orient Express Poster
3b3c9b35-91d8-5460-af41-e16d0268e789.short_description: The Orient Express, owned by the Wagon-Lits Company, connected Paris and Istanbul between 1883 and 1977. French, German, Austrian and Ottoman diplomats and civil servants were on board for its first journey. In the early years, the travellers stayed in different hotels in Istanbul but starting from 1895, passengers stayed exclusively in Pera Palace, which was bought by the Wagon-Lits Company. The Orient Express did not run during World War I, from 1914 to 1918.

3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.name: Map of the Beirut–Damascus railway
3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.short_description: This map shows the railway line connecting Beirut and Damascus. The table on the right shows the distance between each city along horse tracks.
3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury

3cc5829d-ae99-58ec-bc85-707e431d5db4.name: *Edward Jenner*, Marble Group by Giulio Monteverde
3cc5829d-ae99-58ec-bc85-707e431d5db4.short_description: Giulio Monteverde was an Italian sculptor who started carving wooden crucifixes and then moved on to sculpture during his years at the Academy of Fine Arts in Genoa. In 1865 Monteverde moved to Rome to study at the Academy of St. Luke. The sculpture of Edward Jenner (1749-1823) represents the British physician and naturalist inoculating for the first time, on his own son, the smallpox vaccine that he invented. This work was initially rejected by the Academy of St. Luke, entrusted with selecting works of art for the International Exposition in Vienna, and then exhibited in it thanks to an influential friend of the artist. The plaster cast of Jenner won the gold medal in Vienna. The engraving celebrates Monteverde's deeds. Chroniclers report that in 1878 the marble version of the group sculpture was awarded a huge prize at the International Exhibition in Paris: a gold medal and a hearty public welcome.
3cc5829d-ae99-58ec-bc85-707e431d5db4.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.

3cd5a4c9-7c30-53cb-877b-5bf9e71bca5b.name: *One Thousand and One Nights: Arabic fairytales tanslated by Galland, illustrated by the best French artists…*
3cd5a4c9-7c30-53cb-877b-5bf9e71bca5b.short_description: The *One Thousand and One Nights* played an important role in bringing the East and the West closer together. Galland was its first French translator, translating with much liberty the tales that he had been able to understand in the early 18th century. The translated One Thousand and One Nights were extremely successful, and became the subject of a variety of art forms, both allowing Europeans to become better acquainted with the Arab world, but also forming the basis for lasting stereotypes.

3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.name: Italian Workers Friendly Society (Tunis)
3d30eac6-fec9-5efa-aa61-82d8011a50af.short_description: The Italian Workers Friendly Society was only one of the many organizations that the Italian migrants set up in Tunisia, ranging from the Chamber of Commerce, to Masonic Lodges, to religious organisations, to cultural associations and political groups.

3dfa891b-481b-5a43-b37c-1a41ad7c72c1.name: Resistance to the occupation at Oued Zarga
3dfa891b-481b-5a43-b37c-1a41ad7c72c1.short_description: This photograph shows Tunisians attacking the train station at Oued Zarga. The Tunisian resistance caused the French troops many problems as they advanced towards Tunis, where they hoped to force the bey to accept the French protectorate. The attack at the Oued Zarga station, a few hundred kilometres to the west of Tunis, is an example of this. The station itself, which was built by the French, became a symbol through which Tunisians attacked French interests.
3dfa891b-481b-5a43-b37c-1a41ad7c72c1.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
3dfa891b-481b-5a43-b37c-1a41ad7c72c1.author: Bechir Yazidi

3f21696b-6178-5310-a618-3b1cbb1ec3d6.name: *Shéhérazade*
3f21696b-6178-5310-a618-3b1cbb1ec3d6.short_description: George Auriol, the typographer renamed after his creations, was a multitalented artist, and thus in his work he reflected many different influences of the late 19th century. As an artist and musician, he was interested in the different graphic movements, as is clear from this image: the theme is clearly "Oriental", but the composition of the piece borrows characteristics from Japanese aesthetics and Art Nouveau.

3f284929-6dd8-5a5b-9540-23005e47ac6c.name: Colonial school in Paris, project of M. Maurice Yvon
3f284929-6dd8-5a5b-9540-23005e47ac6c.short_description: In 1885, the French diplomat Auguste Pavie brought thirteen young Khmers to Paris so that they could see France. This "Cambodian mission" was soon transformed into a colonial school which accepted young students of French, Cambodian or African origins in order to train the future civil servants of the colonies. Over first two, then three, years the students studied a variety of languages, French law, and ethnology. in 1895 the architect Maurice Yvon, son of an Orientalist painter, was appointed as the architect for a specialist school on 2 Rue de l'Observatoire. Insipired by "neo-Moorish" architecture, the resulting structure became a key example of "colonial art".

3f842425-2ace-59ff-ad9e-176b0b58c8f7.name: *Société les Affréteurs Réunis* \[…\] *Weekly, individual direct services from Rouen and Bordeaux-Bayonne to Algeria and Tunisia, and vice versa.*
3f842425-2ace-59ff-ad9e-176b0b58c8f7.short_description: In Algeria and Tunisia, the French colonisers developed viticulture, cereal farming, and the extraction of minerals for export to France. The transportation of these goods took place by boat. Various firms emerged specifically for the transportation of this type of product, providing specialised ships and regular shipments between North Africa and the major French Atlantic ports. This map indicates the ports in Tunisia and Algeria and the railway networks connecting them (Oranais network, etc.).

401e4018-e1ee-5a6d-87f6-467eb15b5da9.name: Oriental Festival at the Turin Exhibition, 1911
401e4018-e1ee-5a6d-87f6-467eb15b5da9.short_description: In 1911 the city of Turin organized an International Exhibition in the Valentino park, on the banks of the Po River. Beyond the Isabella Bridge another huge park was built to house entertainment and attractions. One of the most popular attractions was the so-called "Kermesse Orientale", in which the public experienced the illusion of making a journey through the different parts of the Eastern world. Five new areas were built, according to photographs taken at the time. The first one represented Arabian, Egyptian, Tunisian and Turkish environments while the fourth area reproduced Japan and India. The park also showcased a harem, a mosque and a Moorish school and the visitors could enjoy belly dancing shows and walks on camelback.
401e4018-e1ee-5a6d-87f6-467eb15b5da9.holder: Central Institute for Ethno-Anthropology, National Museum of Arts and Popular Traditions

409e4adf-c1cd-577f-9523-9ffc50214d63.name: 'Ethnographic Exhibition' [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
409e4adf-c1cd-577f-9523-9ffc50214d63.short_description: Colonel Le Clerc organized an ethnographic gallery inside his own museum of artillery for the International Exhibition of Paris in 1878. He arranged 72 examples of warriors coming from almost every part of the world in a three-room exhibit. These characters were modelled from actual examples and resembled Arabic, Australian, African and Indian people with costumes and features. The exhibition paid great attention to facial renderings and the physical appearance of the warriors.

40b694ae-445b-54d8-b559-e424f0a605c7.name: *Alexander Karatheodori Pasha (1833–1906)*
40b694ae-445b-54d8-b559-e424f0a605c7.short_description: Portrait of Alexander Karatheodori Pasha. He was born in 1833 in the Greek quarter, Phanar, in Constantinople and served as leading diplomat (Premier Plénipotentiaire) of the Ottoman Empire at the 1878 Congress of Berlin. With the consent of the Ottoman government, Austro-Hungarian troops occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina.
keywords: Alexander Karatheodori Pasha;Congress of Berlin; Bosnia

40e07960-2c59-5c21-8ff8-0aa9645bf0eb.name: Postcards showing Romanian tourists in Egypt
40e07960-2c59-5c21-8ff8-0aa9645bf0eb.short_description: In the 19th century, North Africa was mostly known to Romanians from geography schoolbooks and newspaper articles. However, starting from the middle of the 19th century there are information about wealthy Romanians who visited North African countries, some of them recounting in their memoirs their African experiences. For example, Romanian poet and politician Vasile Alecsandri visited in September-October 1853 the Moroccan ports of Tangier and Tétouan and published his impressions in a Romanian literary periodical. A bit more than half a century later, four Romanian students entered an international competition for travelling by foot 100,000 km. In July 1911 they reached Egypt, where they visited Cairo, the pyramids, the Valley of the Kings, Memphis, Luxor, Karnak, Aswan, the Abu Simbel temples.

40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.name: *Bedouin of the Houran*
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.short_description: The constant movement of large Bedouin confederations regularly impacted on the history of the Middle East, in particular when it intersected with settled societies and cities. The bedouins of Hauran lived in the Hauran plain in what is now SW Syria/ NW Jordan at the time. The Sheikh of the Hauran bedouins was employed by the Ottoman pasha of Damascus to collect tribute from all tribes in the area and help in its defence. Philip Meeder was a British wood engraver, who died in 1913. The image is taken from ’Picturesque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt’, Charles William Wilson ed., 1881. The accompanying text in the book reads: 'A bedouin of the Haurân. Bedouins occupy the north-west district of the Haurân; the plain is inhabited by peasants, and the Druses for many centuries have colonised the mountain range.
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
40ef2328-28fd-59f1-96b3-b75abf4e6c58.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

40f40e78-356d-5bdf-a281-3045eb71b83b.name: Hammam-el-Lif, Tunis. Seaside resorts and thermal springs
40f40e78-356d-5bdf-a281-3045eb71b83b.short_description: Hammam el-Lif is a seaside town near Tunis. In 1750, Ali II Bey of Tunis had a pavilion built by the thermal springs, which Hussein II Bey then completed in 1826.

412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.name: Jars from the Company of Glass and Mosaic of Venice and Murano [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.short_description: “The Chronicle of the Universal Exhibition of Paris” of 1878 celebrates the city of Murano’s commercial success in glass production. A large number of these objects reside in the collection of the Museum of Industrial Arts in Rome (M.A.I.), now part of the acquisitions of the National Museum of Antique Art on display at Palazzo Barberini. M.A.I. was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. These jars were manufactured by the famous glass company Salviati, founded in 1866 and established in Venice and Murano. In presenting these objects they claimed the rebirth of a long-forgotten antique art and the rebirth of glass industries in Italy. Tomb excavations brought to light a series of vases. New objects based on those excavated were made on the occasion of the International Exhibition in Paris in 1878.

412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.author: Marina Minozzi

416183bd-8afc-5737-8b32-4fcbb3e2e553.name: Ali ben Ghedhahem's seal
416183bd-8afc-5737-8b32-4fcbb3e2e553.short_description: This seal, dating to 1864, belonged to 'Ali ben Ghedhahem, an educated man and the son of a qadi from the Kasserine region. He was one of the biggest figures in an insurrection triggered by the issuing of a decree to double taxes in Mejba, April 1864. The revolt started in the west, but quickly spread to the whole regency, with the exception of just a few coastal towns. However, it was soon qashed, and the violent suppression the people were subjected was not forgotten until the mid-20th century. The legendary hero 'Ali ben Ghedhahem was arrested and convicted.
416183bd-8afc-5737-8b32-4fcbb3e2e553.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
416183bd-8afc-5737-8b32-4fcbb3e2e553.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: Ali Bin Ghedham; Kasserine region; 1864 revolt

41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.name: Refugees' documents for refuge house after the population exchange
41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.short_description: The 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey was based upon religious identity, and involved the Greek Orthodox citizens of Turkey and the Muslim citizens of Greece. The "Convention Concerning the Exchange of Greek and Turkish Populations" was signed at Lausanne, Switzerland, on 30 January 1923, by the governments of Greece and Turkey. These are refugees' documents for the Papoukidis family's stay at a refuge house.
41adce0c-3867-5629-8e66-064e9b952e0c.holder: Population Exchange Museum (The Foundation of Lausanne Treaty Emigrants)

42290171-ded6-5da8-9103-76fb7763204e.name: *The Attack of the Enemy’s Cavalry at Shinaass January 2nd, 1810*
42290171-ded6-5da8-9103-76fb7763204e.short_description: This image, recorded by a British soldier, who participated in the campaign to destroy the Qawasim's economic hegemony in the Lower Gulf, shows a group of Arab fighters, those on horseback carrying lances, those on foot swords, engaged in fierce combat outside the fortress of Shinas, a Qawasim stronghold on the east coast the British turned to after destroying their bases in Ras al Khaimah and on the Persian coast. Seemingly endless rows of British artillery and infantry are approaching from the beach on the right, with the mast of the British frigates clearly visible at sea. For their attack on the east coast postions of the Qawasim, the British enlisted the support of Omani forces, and it is presumably them that are engaging the mounted Qawasim fighters in this image. British eye witnesses report that the Qawasim fought extremely bravely and obstinately, preferring death to surrender. Nevertheless, the overwhelming military machine of the British eventually took Shinas, with at least 400 Qawasim casualities.
42290171-ded6-5da8-9103-76fb7763204e.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

433df55d-0327-5977-a447-ca5420a7ce29.name: Laënnec examining a patient at the Necker Hospital in 1816
433df55d-0327-5977-a447-ca5420a7ce29.short_description: The 19th century saw a number of important advances in the medical field. René Laënnec (1781–1926) was a French doctor who invented the stethoscope, allowing him to improve medical diagnoses by listening to patients' chests. Doctors were thus able to analyse sounds inside the body, and link them to illnesses such as tuberculosis, which was very common in the 19th century.

43466c72-e5b9-5030-8983-576a5a27f879.name: Alexander I Obrenovic, King of Serbia (1876–1903)
43466c72-e5b9-5030-8983-576a5a27f879.short_description: Portrait of Alexander I Obrenovic, King of Serbia (1876–1903) as a young man. Between the abdication of his father in 1889 and his proclamation as a king in 1893, his mother Natalija Obrenovic ruled as a regent. Being a close ally of Austria, he became Serbian King in 1893. In 1894 Alexander abolished the liberal constitution of Serbia. In 1900 he married Draga Masin, a former lady-in-waiting of his mother. This marriage was very unpopular and weakened the political position of the king. In 1903 he and his wife were murdered by a group of Serbian officers.
keywords: Edmund Count Szecheny; Budapest; Hungary; Istanbul, Ottoman empire; fire brigade

43887649-28e4-5e71-ad7d-9a1cc8750dfc.name: *Art exhibition at school, 12–25 June, 1904*
43887649-28e4-5e71-ad7d-9a1cc8750dfc.short_description: The introduction of art as a primary school subject was a long and difficult process. Linear drawing was introduced first with a utilitarian objective. From 1879, teaching art became mandatory due to a standardization of teaching practices, and specialised teachers were recruited for this purpose. From the early 20th century onwards art became, supposedly, the art of depicting reality. Various organisations also pushed for the democratisation of art in schools. This poster shows a school student taking interest in famous paintings, such as those by Millet.

441fd91e-6a8d-5ba0-b0fb-73ae59155d8a.name: *Voyage Dans Le Levant*
441fd91e-6a8d-5ba0-b0fb-73ae59155d8a.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

443b06f0-b14c-5ef9-9ab2-20b5d7d56003.name: *Clothes for prisoners of war. Charitable organisation attached the French \[Red Cross\]. Donations both in cash and in kind should be delivered to the organisation's headquarters, at 63 Avenue des Champs-Elysées.*
443b06f0-b14c-5ef9-9ab2-20b5d7d56003.short_description: Throughout the First World War, many charitable organisations came to the aid of soldiers and civilian populations in occupied territories. They carried out poster campaigns or published appeals in the press to obtain donations. This poster depicts a military prisoner of war's sadness as he writes to his loved ones. The Red Cross supervised these charitable partnerships in order to ensure the safe arrival of the donations in "enemy" territory.
keywords: Hygiene; Red Cross; First World War

4543ccbf-dceb-5300-941b-8c2f10ba3b29.name: The port of Galaţi
4543ccbf-dceb-5300-941b-8c2f10ba3b29.short_description: After the Russian annexation of Bessarabia (the eastern part of Moldavia) in 1812 and until the restoration by Russia of Southern Bessarabia (1856), Galați remained Moldavia’s only port on the Danube. Understanding the city’s importance for Moldavia’s economy and wanting to ensure its development, prince Mihail Sturdza, who was appointed ruler of Moldavia by the Sublime Porte in 1834, issued in 1836 an act stipulating that Galați was to be a free port (with no or few customs duties) starting with March 1837. Also, a new neighborhood was to be built based on modern urban planning prescriptions and Galați received the right to organize annually five national fairs, during which traders from everywhere could sell any type of products.

460ebced-3992-593a-a42e-32453e973f11.short_description: The subjects of this piece, drawn from life, are men from the west of Algeria. Although we know that Chassériau's main source of inspiration in Algeria was the city of Constantine, he also spent some time in Algiers with his uncle the architect Frédéric Chassériau, who had been employed by Napoléon III to build up the city's seafront. The artist's keen attention to detail is highlighted by his authentic rendition of his subjects' dress and his occasional use of Arabic in his annotations.

46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.name: Bond of 100 francs issued by the Caisse Générale de Secours et de Bienfaisance Israélite de Tunis, in order to raise funds for the construction of a new synagogue in Tunis, and bought by Leone Moreno
46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.short_description:
The construction of the Great Synagogue in Tunis had a long and complicated history. In 1883, the Bey granted a plot of land on which to build the temple to the Italian Jewish physician and president of the Alliance Israélite Universelle of Tunis, Giacomo Castelnuovo. However, the synagogue was ultimately built on a different lot, acquired thanks to a private donation. In the first years of the 20th century, different projects were discussed. The synagogue was finally built in the 1930s.  
  
Leone Moreno (Tunis 1852 – Tunis 1950) was a successful Italian entrepreneur. He belonged to a Jewish family that had migrated from Livorno (Tuscany) to Tunis around 1830. He was awarded honours both by the Italian King (Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia) and by the Bey of Tunis (Nichan Iftikhar).
46d97a8f-bb71-5869-a2ce-ba8b09411232.author: Massimo Sanacore

This vase came from the church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción in Hornos (Jaén) and it was acquired by the National Museum of Archaeology in 1875. 477e3472-eb64-5968-9da0-4243b0453c73.name: *The Great Hall of the Musée Assyrien in the Louvre*
477e3472-eb64-5968-9da0-4243b0453c73.short_description: In May 1847, the world's first " Musée Assyrien" was opened at the Louvre. This was enabled by the arrival of 37 enormous bas-reliefs discovered by Paul-Émile Botta (1802–1870), the French consul in Mosul, at the site of Khorsabad. Botta, a diplomat, doctor, explorer and archaeologist, organised excavations in the hope of rediscovering Nineveh and its Assyrian monuments, and thus brought about the discovery of Khorsabad which in turn aided and accelerated the deciphering of Cuneiform in Mesopotamia. The "Musée Assyrien" pictured here was a great success and  attracted much attention on its opening in Paris in 1847.

483aa52a-ff95-52c4-b7ab-c693f1780161.name: Map of the Red Sea by Jean Baptiste D’Anville, Paris, 1765
483aa52a-ff95-52c4-b7ab-c693f1780161.short_description:
The French geographer and cartographer Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d’Anville was born in Paris in 1697 and died in 1782 and was well known for his significant contribution to European map-making. In 1754 he became an elected member of the l'Academie Royale des Belles-Lettres where he held the position of geographer and was appointed first geographer to the King of France in 1773.  
This large copperplate-engraved map of the Red Sea is entitled: ‘*Golfe Arabique ou Mer Rouge Par le Sr. d'Anville de l'Academie Royale des Belles-Lettres, et de celle des Sciences de Petersbourg, Secretaire de S.A.S. Mgr. le Duc d'Orleans, MDCCLXV*’. It marks: ‘*Le Caire*’ (Cairo), ‘*Medine ou Iatrib Iathrippa*’ (Medina), ‘*Mt Ohhud*’ (Mount Uhud), ‘*Giddah*’ (Jedda), ‘*La Mekke Maco-raba*’ (Mecca), ‘*Mt Arafat*’ (Mount Arafat) and a dotted line showing ‘*Limites du Territoire de la Mekke et de Medine*’ (the extent of the territories of Mecca and Medina).  
D’Anville was a classical scholar and used ancient texts, including those in ancient Greek to help compile his maps; he was also certainly aware of some Arabic words and read Arabic literature in translation. In his important personal project entitled ‘*Mémoires sur l'Egypte ancienne et moderne, suivis d'une description du Golfe Arabique ou de la Mer Rouge*’ printed in 1766, d’Anville notes that *Maco-raba* is a term used by Ptolemy and he goes on (a year later than our map) to analyse the Red Sea in sixty pages. The reference to *Maco-raba* (Makoraba) to describe Mecca is indeed generally considered to be the classical name given to Mecca by Ptolemy in his *Guide to Geography*, although this is a contested attribution; d’Anville also uses the Ptolemaic ‘*Lathrippa*’ (Yathrib) to describe Medina. The Red Sea was of great interest during the eighteenth century, it being an opportunity to explore Egypt as well as the broader ancient world.

4a2a96ac-fddb-5683-9208-73c5deb06b72.short_description: Italian immigrants in Tunisia gave life to a vibrant press. Between 1838 and 1956, 123 Italian periodicals of different type were published in the country. *L’Unione* was the most successful and politically influential among them.

4acd8717-82fe-538c-b4c9-53b16ce962bb.name: The plan of Haydarpaşa Train Station
4acd8717-82fe-538c-b4c9-53b16ce962bb.short_description: The original plan of Haydarpaşa Train Station, viewed from northern frontage. In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects, Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu, to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.
