b97bcb71-a957-5608-9199-9926745d01bd.short_description: On the occasion of the International Exhibition in Turin in 1911 the Talmone Company built an Egyptian Pavilion resembling an Egyptian temple. The inside of the Pavilion shows details inspired by Egyptian motifs and related to the company’s name. Items highlight the taste of the age for Egyptian and oriental objects. The stained glass design in the Pavilion was taken from a postcard design. This picture, showing a stunning view of a caravan travelling across the desert and already used for the Exhibition in Turin in 1898, is now employed to promote the logo "Chocolate of the Pyramids".

ba4a9d77-759d-50a9-9165-61cb49c132a4.short_description: This lithograph by Théodore Frère shows the "Jennée" alley, beneath the Dey of Algiers' former residence, the "Janina". Both the palace and the alley were destroyed in 1853.

bab7404e-f6da-51e5-bfe3-7f236f4ef2b2.name: *Wadi el-Tuffah*
bab7404e-f6da-51e5-bfe3-7f236f4ef2b2.short_description: In this image, a Palestinian lady uses a traditional spinning wheel for cotton. 19th-century Palestine became an increasingly viable, agricultural producer of cotton, whose importance on the world market was steadily increasing. Mainly supplying European countries  Palestine's cotton became a key commodity. 6% of its cultivated land was given up for its production. Throughout the 1860s, concerted efforts were made to meet the ever growing demand, but as early as the 1870s, the industry, which was merely based on expanded cultivation rather than industrialisation, declined again.This print originally appeared on page 192 in Charles William Wilson's  'Pituresque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt, published between 1881 and 1884. The caption reads: ''Wady et Tuffah, commonly called the vale of Eshcol. The peasants grouped in the foreground are under the southern branches of Abraham's oak. In the distance the minaret of the great mosque of Sheikh Ali Bakka, Hebron, may be distinguished'.
bab7404e-f6da-51e5-bfe3-7f236f4ef2b2.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

baca824e-062d-5426-b385-13a5074e8755.name: View of Livorno from the Lighthouse. On the right, one can see the so-called 'Turkish graveyard' highlighted in green
baca824e-062d-5426-b385-13a5074e8755.short_description: In 1762, Muslims living in Livorno were granted a plot of land outside the city walls, near the beach, to build a graveyard (highlighted in green in the lithography). The graveyard remained in use until the second half of the 19th century. A Muslim graveyard existed in Livorno even before the 18th century. A significant Muslim community lived in town. Its first members were captives taken to Italy as slaves. Muslim traders settled in town as well. In 1856, the graveyard was enlarged and surrounded by walls. In 1872 it was demolished to build a road and some of the graves were moved to the city graveyard.
baca824e-062d-5426-b385-13a5074e8755.author: Daniela Tazzi

bae5f080-ad41-5249-82bc-b0f3de4d1129.name: *Médailles d'honneur d'or et de 1er mérite* \[…\] Biberon-Robert, flexible, patented \[…\] Only the very best doesn't let your child go thirsty
bae5f080-ad41-5249-82bc-b0f3de4d1129.short_description: As infant mortality was still commonplace in the 19th century, the need to instil young parents with an understanding of hygiene in order to counter child illness quickly became clear. This poster advertises a new child's feeding bottle, showcasing its high quality and foregrounding an image of a healthy baby.

bb75e12c-a4e6-5ac9-952c-ce0d0a5fbea2.name: *Constantinople et le Bosphore de Thrace*
bb75e12c-a4e6-5ac9-952c-ce0d0a5fbea2.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

bb8237ee-e92e-5329-9529-6fd346236dd0.name: *Jaffa from the Camp of Ibrahim Pasha*
bb8237ee-e92e-5329-9529-6fd346236dd0.description: This print shows the Ibrahim Pasha camp at Jaffa during the Egyptian – Ottoman War (1830–1833). Muhammad Ali Pasha demanded control of Greater Syria for the Ottoman Empire. Ali sent his army into Syria under the command of his son Ibrahim Pasha. The Egyptian navy landed at Jaffa.
bb8237ee-e92e-5329-9529-6fd346236dd0.author: Carmen Linés Viñuales

bcebbe38-8019-5c28-b4b7-8f04a8b1d7be.name: Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848)
bcebbe38-8019-5c28-b4b7-8f04a8b1d7be.short_description: Portrait of Ibrahim Pasha (1789–1848). As the best General under his father Muhammad 'Ali Pasha, he fought successfully against the Wahhabites, the Ottoman Army and the Greeks. In 1831 he conquered Syria and governed it until 1841. In 1848 he deposed his senile father and was declared Vice King of Egypt by Sultan Abdülmecid I.

bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.name: *The Library of Hadrian*
bd196d3c-3ad7-5a3c-a7bf-f9e67e2fa612.short_description: This representation is entitled *Painted Stoa*, referring to the colonnade (stoa) with monumental columns depicted on the right side of the picture. Nineteenth-century visitors to Athens referred to this monument by various names, such as Painted Stoa of Hadrian or Gymnasium, for its true identity was not discovered until after 1884, when systematic excavations commenced in the area of the Roman Agora (Forum Romanum). Recent archaeological investigation shows that this imposing colonnade is part of the propylon of the Library of Hadrian. Depicted at the edge of the propylon-incorporated in two columns- is a small Byzantine church. This is Hagioi Asomatoi sta Skalia (Incorporeal Saints at the Steps) of the eleventh century, and was demolished before the end of the nineteenth century, falling victim to the antiquarian extremism of ‘purifying archaeological sites’. The works of the artist-travellers who flooded into Greece during the nineteenth century are tangible testimonies not only to the illustrious past, but also to the landscape.

bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.name: Villa Maria, in Tunis, the mansion of Luigi Rey, the son of a migrant from Piedmont (Italy)
bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.short_description: Luigi Rey was the son of Italian immigrants Giuseppe Rey (1808-1897), of Piedmont and Adelaide Baldacci, of Tuscany. In 1836, Giuseppe Rey was dispatched to Tunis by his employer, a construction company from Genoa, to work in the Bardo Palace (the official residence of the Bey of Tunis). After completing the contract Giuseppe decided to stay in Tunisia, where he continued to work at the service of the Bey. Together with his three children (Luigi, Antonio and Pio), Giuseppe Rey set up a construction company that continued after his death. Predominantly with his brothers but at times on his own, Luigi Rey built a variety of private and public edifices, including the Tunisia Palace Hotel (designed by architect Resplandy).

be90f64f-96f3-5dda-8345-68adf8244431.name: *Commercial port. Marseille*
be90f64f-96f3-5dda-8345-68adf8244431.short_description: Frédéric Alexianu (aka F. Hugo d'Alesi) was a painter who quickly became specialised in advertisement posters for different kinds of transports, and in educational maps. This poster, aimed at primary school children, uses the example of Marseille to illustrate a trading port. The artist draws attention to the different commercial activities undertaken here, in addition to the transport of passengers on an ocean liner. The port of Marseille was the most important Mediterranean port in France, as it facilitated a great number of commercial exchanges with the French colonies in North Africa.

bee6cdea-7a07-512a-8073-61c3a5461987.name: *La Sahrienne: Arab dance for piano*
bee6cdea-7a07-512a-8073-61c3a5461987.short_description: The rise of "turkeries" in the 18th century is a good example of the influence of the widespread fascination with the "Orient" on music. In the 19th century, this Orientalism also influenced others art forms, such as painting and photography. Musical motifs started using "oriental" motifs once again in the early 20th century.

bf285df3-f538-57bf-9807-cad97e61acd5.short_description: This political and commercial map, drawn after the Congress of Berlin (1878), shows maritime and railway routes, as well as the travel time they require.

bf8ccf55-0b9f-51ab-833d-046d658d52ad.name: *Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey* (1784–1839)
bf8ccf55-0b9f-51ab-833d-046d658d52ad.short_description:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.
keywords: Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey; Egypt; Janissary; Konya; Ibrahim Pasha; Muhammad Ali; Greece

c05efb28-37e3-563c-be40-ec598ca0daf7.name: Popular resistance to the occupation
c05efb28-37e3-563c-be40-ec598ca0daf7.short_description: Following the signing of the Treaty of Bardo many Tunisian towns declared their opposition to the act and set up a fierce resistance. This was the case in the town of Sfax, which withstood a six-month siege by sealing up, in the dead of night, the holes French bombings had created in the town walls. This image shows the end of the siege as the French forces invaded the town.

c0647b9c-1ac0-53b5-a15b-d5505d2f8137.name: An Italian booklet printed in Tunis in 1898 by Socialist and Anarchist Typography on the trial against the Italian anarchist leader Enrico Malatesta
c0647b9c-1ac0-53b5-a15b-d5505d2f8137.short_description:
Enrico Malatesta (1853-1932) was one of the most important Italian anarchist leaders and theorists. He spent a good part of his life in exile in different countries (including Argentina, Egypt, France, Lebanon, Siria, England and the United States). In 1882, he went to Egypt to support the revolt of Ahmad Urabi and was arrested by British authorities. In 1897, he was living in Ancona, in Central Italy, when he was arrested and put on trial. After serving seven months in prison, he was placed in internal exile on the island of Lampedusa (south of Sicily) from where, in 1899, he fled to Tunisia, then to Malta, then on to England.  
Italians in Tunisia set up a number of associations, political groups, newspapers, and cultural institutions of different political persuasions.
c0647b9c-1ac0-53b5-a15b-d5505d2f8137.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
c0647b9c-1ac0-53b5-a15b-d5505d2f8137.author: Giulia Barrera

c0d68bf3-fc29-5afb-9f0b-b36ef1a39350.name: "Workers' pensions"
c0d68bf3-fc29-5afb-9f0b-b36ef1a39350.short_description: In 1910, a new law on "workers and farmers' pensions" introduced a compulsory insurance scheme. Before this, however, life was very different and many workers lived a very difficult old age, without financial support. The question of workers and farmers' pensions was one of the key electoral questions of the time therefore, as it concerned the majority of the population and those in power feared the social unrest it could trigger. This comical drawing mocks Alexandre Millerand (1859–1943), a socialist politician who forgot all his promises as soon as the elections were over.
keywords: Precarity; workers; pensions; elections; cartoon; caricature

c17a9d7b-cb1a-5e3b-a30d-5c5dfc42e18d.name: *Valtice/Feldsberg, Liechtenstein Chateau, Frontage*
c17a9d7b-cb1a-5e3b-a30d-5c5dfc42e18d.description:
The design presents the original state of the frontage (right) and its redecoration by Antonio Beduzzi, an imperial theatre engineer and designer. Beduzzi based his design on the existing state, supplementing the frontage area with layered planimetric ornamentation. A pivotal role was played by sculpted decoration and military emblems associated with the military career of the count.  
Detailed decorative drawings are part of an important phase in the history of the Valtice/Feldsberg, Liechtenstein Chateau. The chateau, residence of one of the most prominent court families in the Habsburg monarchy, Valtice, was constructed on the border of Lower Austria and Moravia in the first half of the 17th century, with finishing touches added towards the end of the century. Its construction was associated with a number of leading architects active in Vienna (Giovanni Battista Carlone, Giovanni Giacomo Tencalla, Giovanni Tencalla, Giovanni Pietro Tencalla, Domenico Martinelli, Pietro Giulietti and others). Yet the final phase of the construction, during which the building acquired its present appearance, only came about during the period of the counts Anton Florián and Josef Jan.  
Anton Josef Ospel, the architect of the first part of the final phase between 1713 and1722, produced a bold design merging the newly modified older sections with new outbuildings and administration tracts. In the following building phase, a new count put a halt to the further spread of the construction and concentrated on decoration of the interior and frontages of the main *corps de logis*, for which he hired Antonio Beduzzi. Beduzzi created a series of high quality drawings for the count that served as template *modellos* for the final building modifications.
c17a9d7b-cb1a-5e3b-a30d-5c5dfc42e18d.short_description: The residence of a prominent Habsburg court family saw a major reconstruction in the 18th century under a new architect, the imperial theatre engineer and designer Antonio Beduzzi. He created a series of drawings that served as templates for the final building modifications.
c17a9d7b-cb1a-5e3b-a30d-5c5dfc42e18d.obtention: The drawing comes from a large collection of designs owned by the Brno architect František Antonín Grimm. Until 1945 it was located in the Rájec nad Svitavou Chateau, from whence it was transferred to the Museum of Applied Arts, Brno. In 1961, when the Moravian Gallery was established, the drawing became part of the gallery’s collection of historical drawings and graphic art.

c25b97af-3b31-51d4-8c86-07d5d3f06ecd.name: Egyptian House in the Trocadero Park [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
c25b97af-3b31-51d4-8c86-07d5d3f06ecd.short_description: The structure of an Egyptian home was considered particularly interesting and was rebuilt inside the Trocadero Park. The idea and the execution of the house were supported by the famous French Egyptologist Mariette-Bey, who was responsible for numerous excavations along the Valley of Nile and was the founder of the Cairo Museum. This work differs from the one presented by Mariette at the Exhibition in 1867 and was meant to represent a common living building. One room was dedicated to the opening of the Suez Canal and numerous photos and albums provided documentary evidence of Egyptian fashion, oases and travel memories.

c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.name: Rome Exhibition 1911 (Piazza d'Armi) – Sicilian Pavilion
c369fdd9-b766-5049-9f4f-a257d2df3d50.short_description: Within the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911 and related to the celebrations for the 50th anniversary of the Unification of Italy, a "Forum of Regions" was arranged in the Piazza d’Armi. The architect Ernesto Basile (1857–1932), author of the project for the Sicilian Pavilion, took inspiration from the Arab-Norman architecture in Sicily, in particular from Zisa Palace, the church of Saint John of the Hermits and the Cathedral of Monreale. On the outside, the building looked like a cube with plain walls decorated with blind pointed arches and battlements on top. Doors and windows show pointed arch as well. At the sides of the facades two small towers topped by a small small dome give to the palace a striking oriental look. On the inside, there was an open space with columns topped by capitals, walls decorated with mosaics and majolicas, and fountains.

c3e7eb63-5667-5bab-9f33-9ffa073e393f.name: *The Worship of Pallas Athene*
c3e7eb63-5667-5bab-9f33-9ffa073e393f.description: The scene shows a statue of Pallas Athene, goddess of wisdom, on an altar. A group of *putti* are garlanding the statue, while their companions pour incense into an offering vessel. The drawing was inspired by Paul Troger's time in Italy, a period of several years. Together with Martin van Meytens among others, he “studied ancient monuments in the vicinity of Rome with such unceasing diligence that very often we only made do, for days, with bread and water in order to continue with our study without disturbance”. The artist modelled the central motif on a statue of Pallas Athene from the famous collection of ancient art assembled by Marquis Vincenzo Giustiniani (now in the Vatican Museum, Rome). The statue was also known from a print of 1631 and from pictorial publications on ancient sculpture. Paul Troger employed a subject similar to the Brno drawing in an etching from 1724, the origin of which is provably associated with the artist's stay in Rome. Troger's etching and the Brno drawing resemble the engraving technique of Venetian *peintre-graveur*, using a fine grid for the modelling and to capture transitions in light. Typical examples may be found in the work of Giovanni Battista Tiepolo (1696–1770), a major exponent of Italian *Settecento* painting. The subject of adoration of the goddess of wisdom reflects the growing emphasis placed on education at the time. Troger's unfinished drawing probably served as a template for a print celebrating Wisdom. The principal motif is worked up in detail, while the accompanying figures of *putti* and the landscape in the background are sketched in pencil. Continuous wavy lines give evidence of a swift and expressive drawing manner. The artist was an influential professor of the Vienna Academy and was a leading Central European painter of the 18th century.
c3e7eb63-5667-5bab-9f33-9ffa073e393f.short_description: The drawing of a statue of Pallas Athene was inspired by Paul Troger's long stay in Italy. Its execution resembles Venetian *peintre-graveur*. The unfinished drawing was probably to serve as a template for a print celebrating Wisdom.
c3e7eb63-5667-5bab-9f33-9ffa073e393f.method_for_datation: The determination of the artist is based on a confirmed provenance. Troger's authorship is proven, in particular, by the distinctive faces of the *putti* and the brisk drawing manner.
c3e7eb63-5667-5bab-9f33-9ffa073e393f.obtention: The drawing probably comes from the estate of the sculptor Josef Winterhalder Sr., a friend of Troger. It was donated to the gallery by Mrs Trapp before 1963, and was previously found in the collections of the archivist and historian Jan Petr Cerroni and Mořic Wilhelm Trapp, a curator of the Francis Museum in Brno.

c5af0628-6524-5b0d-a3ae-ef6099a54a96.name: *Encampment of the Awlad Said Mount Sinai 1839*
c5af0628-6524-5b0d-a3ae-ef6099a54a96.short_description: The Awlad Said are a large clan of the Sawalha tribe, traditionally based on Southern Sinai. It was escorts from this tribe that accompanied Roberts during his traversing of the Sinai. This depiction gives a detailed impression of their traditional encampments and tent construction. Situated in a valley sheltered by high, rugged mountain ranges, the encampment consists of severalrows of low, rectangular tent structures with flat roofs. Separating walls and screens within are created by striped, woven textile units. Inhabitants of the camp are seen seated in small groups, engaged in conversation or standing in groups, lances in hand. The men are dressed in headscarfs, gowns and cloaks of varying colour, while the few female figures that appear are cloaked in black abayas, all-enveloping black cloaks. From a ravine in the far background, a long caravan of men and camels approaches the camp.

c5b30d17-788f-5526-9443-d7a3c584472b.name: Italian peasants in Tunisia
c5b30d17-788f-5526-9443-d7a3c584472b.short_description: According to official statistics, in 1921 there were around 4,000 Italian peasants in Tunisia; together with their families they amounted to 15,400 people, or roughly 60 per cent of the Europeans employed in agriculture.

c5d1c4ee-c5dd-5526-a357-f968533cd6be.name: *Semiramis*
c5d1c4ee-c5dd-5526-a357-f968533cd6be.short_description: Staging of *Semiramis* in France, played in a set based on ancient sculptures. There is a mix of Egyptian and Assyrian costume, plus some fantasy.

c60364d0-48c1-5f1e-9f18-2ee410152391.name: Drawing
c60364d0-48c1-5f1e-9f18-2ee410152391.short_description: In 1826, Victor Rousseau, French artist living in political exile in London, was hired by Augusto Ferreira Pinto Basto, son of the Vista Alegre Factory’s founder. Regarding the artistic aspect, his hiring allowed for the introduction of new models and decorations, into the eclectic and romantic spirit of those times, and was essential in providing Vista Alegre’s portfolio with a new aesthetic and formal wealth and exuberance. Along with his pedagogical and artistic contribution in the Factory, Victor Rousseau also left as a legacy an interesting drawing album. The drawing, with scenes from the Factory representing the Aveiro Estuary and river Bôco, calls our attention to the specificities needed for the implementation of an industry in the 19th century. The proximity of the estuary represented not only abundance of water, but also offered easy routes for transporting raw materials and other commodities.
keywords: Victor Rousseau; Factory; Vista Alegre; Aveiro estuary; master of painting

c671443a-8a37-5c35-975f-840074e8db8a.name: *Woman Playing a String Instrument*
c671443a-8a37-5c35-975f-840074e8db8a.short_description: In this painting there is an Ottoman woman in her daily attire with her hair covered by an embroidered and printed kerchief. She plays a string instrument. Music was one of the most popular kinds of amusement in Turkish harems. The lute in particular, and similar string instruments, have always occupied an important place in the lives of women. This picture was used on the cover of a special issue of *Le Figaro Illustré* dedicated to Zonara and published in 1908, and also appeared in *Der'i Se'adet*, a book written by Adolphe Thalasso and illustrated by Zonaro.
keywords: Music; harem; court music; musician; female musician; traditional entertainments

c6c98aa8-0cf8-5f68-9a72-93ac7214dab2.name: *Map of the Royal Cities of Buda and Pest*
c6c98aa8-0cf8-5f68-9a72-93ac7214dab2.description: The *Map of the Royal Cities of Buda and Pest* depicts all the settlements that bordered Buda: the Roman settlement of *Aquincum;* the border with Budafok and a detail of Óbuda (Old Buda). The city of Pest is also identifiable, together with the two suburbs of Terézváros and Erzsébetváros. During the period, as the map shows, the hills of Buda were not forested because, following Ottoman rule, the inhabitants cultivated vineyards instead. The Royal Castle is identifiable, together with the Viziváros (Watertown) and Tabán. Residents were settled mainly within the city walls up until 1700, after which time the suburbs began to be built. At the end of the 18th century, Buda-Pest became increasingly important as the main commercial and agricultural centre and although the diet was held in Pozsony (Bratislava), the two cities of Buda and Pest were the centre for various political movements, Enlightenment thought, the arts and literature, and as a consequence the population increased to 50,000.
c6c98aa8-0cf8-5f68-9a72-93ac7214dab2.short_description: A map of the two cities of Buda and Pest with a more detailed representation of the different parts of the former and a less detailed display of the two suburbs of Pest.
c6c98aa8-0cf8-5f68-9a72-93ac7214dab2.obtention: Purchased from an art dealer in Budapest between the two world wars.

c74178c2-ab9f-5408-9cbb-cf1f4eff394d.name: Press release about Raml Tramway
c74178c2-ab9f-5408-9cbb-cf1f4eff394d.short_description: A press release in the Al-Ahram newspaper regarding the Raml Tramway and related views of the Prime Minister at that time. The tramway of Alexandria was the first method of mass transportation in Egypt and in Africa, and the most common. The tramway began operating in 1860, and is thus considered the oldest tramway in Africa – and among the oldest in the world.

c82a2a26-f746-5771-93c4-6bcceedcab50.name: *Mount Gilboa from Sulem, a woman spinning cotton*
c82a2a26-f746-5771-93c4-6bcceedcab50.short_description: 19th-century Palestine was an increasingly viable, agricultural producer of cotton, whose importance on the world market was steadily increasing. Mainly supplying European countries, cotton became a key commodity. 6% of the cultivated land of Palestine was given up. Throughout the 1860s, concerted efforts were made to meet demand, but as early as the 1870s, the industry, which was merely based on expanded cultivation rather than industrialisation, declined again. This print originally appeared in Vol.1, page 269 of Charles William Wilson's 'Pituresque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt, published between 1881 and 1884. The caption reads: 'Mount Gilboa from Sulem (Shunem). The northern extremity of the range of Jebel Fuku'a (Gilboa) is shown; the highest point is crowned by the sanctuary of Neby Mezar. In the foreground a woman is spinning cotton.

c8dcb99a-4981-58af-a357-22664ca7f472.short_description: With this treaty, the Grand Duke of Tuscany Leopold II and the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Megid Han intended to encourage economic exchanges between the countries. Tuscan citizens and ships were accorded the same privileges that those from other countries had received. The treaty also provided for some tax reduction in favour of Tuscan merchants.

c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.name: *Votes for Women*
c99f4a2d-2d4c-538b-b57e-e1ba93984854.short_description:
This Suffragette poster was created in response to the Liberal Prime Minister Herbert Asquith's suppression of the 1910 Conciliation Bill, which proposed extending the vote in Britain and Ireland to around one million wealthy, property-owning women. It shows King George V painting the text 'We Bow to the Will of the People' onto a poster, whilst a man paints on the King's back, and a Suffragette paints onto the man’s. The cartoon aimed to show how Asquith had gone against the will of Parliament, the elected representatives of the people. The Suffragettes urged male voters to register their protest by voting against Liberal candidates in the next election.  
  
This poster was published by the Woman's Press, who oversaw the publishing and propaganda for the Suffragettes. It was designed by Alfred Pearse, under the pseudonym ‘A. Patriot', Pearse was a dedicated Suffragette supporter and designed many of their posters.

ca6bd475-805d-5b06-a1e3-16bb93242b3b.name: *The interior of the Queen's carriage: meeting between Louis-Philippe and Queen Victoria*
ca6bd475-805d-5b06-a1e3-16bb93242b3b.short_description: Keen on keeping up good relations with the United Kingdom, King Louis-Philippe of France accepted Queen Victoria's invitation in 1844. Accompanied by Guizot and his youngest son, the Duke of Montpensier, he was received lavishly by the English royal family. In 1842, Queen Victoria became the first sovereign to take the train between London and Windsor. Since then, British rail companies had begun setting up carriages especially reserved for the Royal Family. One of the key experiences offered to Louis-Philippe was the opportunity to travel by train in one of these spectacular carriages.
ca6bd475-805d-5b06-a1e3-16bb93242b3b.artist: Lithographer: Jules David; artist: Édouard Pingret

cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.name: *View of Smyrna*
cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.short_description: Both this print and the *View of Constantinople* are based on earlier Western ones, which have been assimilated into the distinctive Athonite topographical style. They are exceptions to the corpus of Athonite prints, since they are of secular subjects. The printmaker was, indeed, active outside Athos, where he executed nonreligious commissions. The subjects relate to the tradition of topographical murals depicting important commercial and cultural centers of the day that decorated the mansions of wealthy merchants by the mid-eighteenth century. Kaldis aimed to supply a wider public with inexpensive works of a decorative nature. The activity of merchants from Lesbos at Smyrna, Constantinople, and the Black Sea on the one hand justified the choice of subject and, on the other, provided the appropriate network in which the multiple printed works could circulate. In order to attract the largest possible clientele, the view is coloured.
cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.author: Papastratos 1990, vol. 2, 578-79, figs. 617-18; Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 508-9, figs. 900-901

cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.name: *Bisotun, geometric drawing of a bas-relief*
cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.short_description: In 1840, the painter Eugène Flandin (1809–1876) and the architect and painter Pascal Coste (1787–1879) were sent on mission to Persia by l'Institut de France in order to write up an inventory of the country's past and contemporary riches, and to renew the political and economic ties between France and Persia. The mission was directed by Édouard de Sercey, who soon returned to France. However, despite the trying conditions, Flandin and Coste were able to stay for two more years and collected an impressive archive documenting the sites they explored. This is a print of one of the bas-reliefs in Mount Behistun (Iran), which  Darius had carved during the 6th century BC.
cb836758-5e12-5a3f-adea-db7c9212b700.artist: Engraver: A. Guillaumet; artist: Pascal-Xavier Coste; author: Eugène Flandin

cc9708c7-7639-577d-908b-b4db3b0e057e.name: Shéhérazade, a ballet by Michel Fokine. Stage sketch.
cc9708c7-7639-577d-908b-b4db3b0e057e.short_description: The Russian choreographer Michel Fokine created the ballet *Shéhérazade* for Rimski-Korsakov's music in Paris in 1910. The tale of Shahrazad was taken from the *One Thousand and One Nights*, which saw constant success in Europe throughout the 19th century.

ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.name: Records of the tests and of the delivery of the yacht Makook III built by the Fratelli Orlando Company (Livorno, Italy) for the Egyptian Khedive Abbas Hilmi
ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.short_description: In 1910, the Khédivé of Egypt contracted the construction of a yacht to the shipyards Cantieri Gallinari of Livorno, Italy. This company went bankrupt and its business was absorbed by the Fratelli Orlando shipyards, also from Livorno. After improving the project, the Fratelli Orlando started building the yacht in 1913 and delivered it to the Khédivé Hilmì Abbas in May 1914. In recognition of the high quality of work on the yacht engineer Giuseppe Orlando was granted the Ottoman decoration of the Order of Osmanieh.
ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.author: Daniela Tazzi

cce9ed43-6802-51d5-8553-802e6dafb35e.name: *Siever's patent pedestrian carriage for Ladies and Gentlemen*
cce9ed43-6802-51d5-8553-802e6dafb35e.short_description: Many different two-wheeled cycles, such as dandy horses and velocipedes, were invented in the early 19th century. Their underlying principle was the parallel use of feet and wheels to propel the vehicle forward. They quickly become very fashionable amongst the European upper classes, who saw them as a source of entertainment, as we can see from this English print. However, it was not until the 20th century, after many alterations (pedals, etc.) that the "bicycle" became a widespread mode of transport.

cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.name: *Vizovice Chateau, Chapel*
cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.description:
The chapel in the south wing of the Vizovice Chateau in the Wallachia region is built into a central layout with three apses and crowned with a cupola. The drawing represents the chapel on a single level. On the left is a pulpit decorated with a relief of the Baptism of Christ, and the high altar with the Assumption of the Virgin Mary with a sarcophagus-shaped tabernacle, figures of Mary's parents, St. Joachim and St. Anne, and a Marian picture carried by angels, the top of which features a monogram of the name “Mary”. The second altar, decorated with consecration crosses, provides a framework for a picture of St. John of Nepomuk. The third field is a design for an oratory with illusionary drapery. In the place of the door is the last of the vaulting joints decorated with tetramorphs of the evangelists with angels carrying the gospels, from the left: Matthew, John (eagle), Mark (lion) and Luke (bull).  
Schweigl's design, with fine ornamentation in Louis XVI style, was executed with only minor changes (the latest of which was in 1777), in accordance with the requirements of the chateau's sponsor Heřman Hannibal of Blümegen (c. 1774), who also endowed the chapel with precious chasubles and liturgical objects that have survived to this day. A relief of the birth of Christ was created for the pulpit, replacing the original design. The decoration of the oratory is much more austere, without the theatre-like curtain.  
The Rococo interior with its relief decoration stands in contrast to the low-key classicist architecture of František Antonín Grimm who trained in Rome, in the studio of Nicolo di Salvi, in France and in Germany. The design bears witness to the versatility of the learned Brno sculptor, Andreas Schweigl. Schweigl did not underestimate the role of the decorator, something that gained in significance towards the end of the century.
cdb325fe-1956-58e5-9130-f95c81512902.short_description: The design shows the versatility of the learned Brno sculptor Andreas Schweigl, who did not underestimate the decorator’s role. The chapel interior, with fine Louis XVI ornamentation, contrasts with the low-key classicist architecture of František Antonín Grimm, who trained in Rome, France and Germany.

ce785e40-77c2-5e37-a375-478e1a61faa0.description: This engraving is an example of an illustration travel book in the 19th century. Thomas Allom (1804–1873), the painter of this engraving, was a topographical illustrator who travelled to East Mediterranean, North Africa and China. Allom was also architect, hence the description of the architectural details in “The interior of a Moorish palace in Alger”.

cf106c3f-4539-5afa-9774-85924fe852cf.name: Book of patterns
cf106c3f-4539-5afa-9774-85924fe852cf.short_description:
Most of the folios are divided into square or rectangular compartments filled with drawings of a wide variety of repeating patterns, often with figural motifs but most with stylised floral elements. There are also rubbings, woodblock prints and a few drawings, mostly of objects and sprays of flowers, some coloured and some occupying a full page. Many patterns were drawn directly on the pages but others were pasted in.  
The designs based on human figures – including dancers, acrobats and mounted riders – are among the most creative. But of greater complexity are some with animals; fish, cobras, birds, elephants, squirrels, lions, tigers, camels and deer are represented. Some of the patterns are inspired by traditional Mughal decorative motifs, while others are European in taste.  
The pattern book had the potential to be of great use to jewellers and enamellers as well craftsmen working in textiles, manuscript illumination, bidri-ware and other metalwork, ceramic paving and marquetry work.

cf1febcd-3ef8-57e3-ad0c-a21a1977147f.name: Trips to Morocco. Oujda via Lalla Marnia. Hôtel Figari […] car service every day […] links to the Tlemcen stagecoach and trains to Western Algeria.

Its inaccuracies bring to light the dominant stereotypes of the time, particularly regarding the depiction of women and their place in Muslim society.

cf466251-56ab-52b7-a4c0-a209a97dcdb0.name: *Ethics by example. From education, great nations are born*
cf466251-56ab-52b7-a4c0-a209a97dcdb0.short_description: In the 19th and 20th centuries, ethics dominated French primary school teaching. The school day began with a lesson in ethics, aimed at training the children to be good parents and good national citizens.

cf6fd523-ce44-5925-8fcb-a5eba1bea0a5.name: General Giuseppe Garibaldi, hero of the Italian national unification, arriving in Tunis in 1834
cf6fd523-ce44-5925-8fcb-a5eba1bea0a5.short_description:
In 1833, Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807-1882) joined Mazzini’s organization, Giovane Italia, a republican group that supported the unification of Italy, and in 1834 he participated in an attempted insurrection. He was sentenced to death by the Kingdom of Sardinia and fled abroad. He spent time in Tunis in the first half of 1835.  
Later, Garibaldi went to South America (1835-1848) where he fought for the independence of different countries. When he came back to Italy he fought to defend the Roman Republic (1849), and in 1860 led a successful expedition of one thousand volunteers in Southern Italy to defeat the Kingdom of Two Sicilies and unify it with Central and Northern Italy.  
During the Italian Risorgimento, several other liberals and supporters of Italian unification were forced to go into exile. Several went to North Africa.
cf6fd523-ce44-5925-8fcb-a5eba1bea0a5.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
cf6fd523-ce44-5925-8fcb-a5eba1bea0a5.author: Giulia Barrera

cf731a2d-eeba-5936-b7db-3a4740cb21ee.name: Print
cf731a2d-eeba-5936-b7db-3a4740cb21ee.short_description:
The English architect Owen Jones designed this menu card for a farewell banquet coinciding with the Paris International Exhibition – or Exposition Universelle – of 1867. International exhibitions played an important role in introducing imported styles of ornament. The design of this card echoes illuminated Persian manuscripts, which Jones included in his book Grammar of Ornament.  
Apart from working as an architect, Jones also designed interiors, wallpapers and textiles. He created the interior for the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, which housed the Great Exhibition of 1851.
cf731a2d-eeba-5936-b7db-3a4740cb21ee.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
keywords: Prints; Entertainment & Leisure; Eating; The Great Exhibition; Menus; Illumination

d0201dc5-b133-5197-929c-a269917b72e1.name: *L'art arabe d'après les monuments du Kaire depuis le VIIè siècle jusqu'à la fin du XVIIIè*
d0201dc5-b133-5197-929c-a269917b72e1.short_description: A publication in three volumes *L'art arabe d'après les monuments du Kaire depuis le VIIè siècle jusqu'à la fin du XVIIIè* is a monumental work by archaeologist and architect Prisse d'Avennes. It was published in parts by V.A. Morel et Cie. from 1869 to 1877. In 200 plates he reproduced illustration on the art and architecture of Islamic Cairo.

d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.name: Italian postcard of colonial propaganda: 'The Turco-Italian War. The Italian governor taking possession of Tripoli'
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.short_description:
In this postcard we see the first Italian public ceremony during the colonial conquest of Libya.  
As Terence Ranger pointed out in his essay “The invention of tradition in colonial Africa” in E. Hobsbawn and T Ranger, *The Invention of Tradition* (Cambridge University Press 1983), public ceremonies were a tool that was much used by colonial powers. Their goal was to grant a public image of legitimacy to colonial domination. In other words, colonial pomp and circumstance were intended to convey to colonial subject a notion of might and “prestige” of the colonisers.
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.holder: State Library of Modern and Contemporary History
d04ab320-9a12-53d1-93fd-cefc444af612.author: Maria Pia Critelli, Giulia Barrera

d07a016a-4cbb-5e3f-8479-fd71b40996a8.name: Exposition in Algiers - façade of the Pavillon des Beaux-Arts, in the Place du Gouvernement
d07a016a-4cbb-5e3f-8479-fd71b40996a8.short_description: In 1800, the first "Algerian" exposition was held in Algiers, in a building built especially for this purpose at the Place du Gouvernement (now Place des Martyrs). However, this was in reality an opportunity for France to advertise the "benefits" of colonialism - pacified and economically improved, Algeria was apparently now able to take interest in the arts. The review magazine therefore decided to prioritise paintings with an Algerian theme, irrespective of whether they had been created there or abroad.

d5146f7c-a989-5ed0-8084-92511311bc67.name: An insurance policy by the company Compagnia Affricana (based in Trieste), for the merchandise transported by the Tuscan brigantine *Otello*, from Alexandria (Egypt) to Livorno (Italy)

d698b39b-7d12-5410-a70f-c142ce18b236.name: *Servet-i Fünun* Journal
d698b39b-7d12-5410-a70f-c142ce18b236.short_description: This is a magazine published by the authors from the *Servet-ı Fünun* (*Edebiyat-ı Cedide*) movement. It was first published as a scientific magazine by Ahmet İhsan Tokgöz, a pupil of Recaizade Mahmud Ekrem, in 1891. Recaizade Mahmud Ekrem agreed with his pupil to turn this magazine into one of literature, so he arranged that Tevfik Fikret, another student of his from Galatasaray High school, would become head of the literature department. This movement came to an end when the magazine was closed after if published an article entitled “Literature and Justice,” translated by Hüseyin Cahit Yalçın, which was taken as hostile to the governance of Abdülhamid II. Members of the *Edebiyat-ı Cedide* movement remained adherent to Diwan literature due to the political situation of the period as well as political suppression. They were not as open to novelties as the first generation of Tanzimat Era and they adopted art for sake of art.

d6cffdd2-cbd5-5bf7-bd67-0a2b5084a2cc.name: In Tunis, the families of the Italian men drafted for the war waiting to get their daily allowance from the Italian government
d6cffdd2-cbd5-5bf7-bd67-0a2b5084a2cc.short_description: According to a booklet published in 1917 by the Tunisian branch of the Dante Alighieri Society and quoted by historian Adriano Salmieri (see his contribution to the volume *Mestieri e professioni degli italiani di Tunisia* – *Métiers et professions des Italiens de Tunisie, a cura di S. Finzi, Tunisi: Finzi*, 2003), by the end of April 1917 11,146 Italians in Tunisia had been drafted for the war, and 700 had died. According to the same source, in 1917 in Tunisia the Italian government was paying daily allowances to almost 5,000 destitute families of drafted soldiers.

d6d5f11a-71c5-5934-871d-7aa7c6836d79.short_description: On his arrival in Egypt, Salt sponsored and recorded the excavations of Captain Giovanni Battista Caviglia at the Giza pyramids and Sphinx. Caviglia discovered new chambers in the Great Pyramid and a lost chapel beneath the head of the Sphinx.

d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.description: At the end of the 19th and during the first decade of the 20th century Pirot kilims served as unavoidable decor in public buildings and in important public manifestations. An official wedding photo of King Alexander Obrenović of Serbia and Queen Draga, shows a royal couple standing on the Pirot kilims, used as floor coverings in this solemn occasion as distinguished national products. The official photograph, taken on 4 August 1900 by the court photographer Milan Jovanović, was issued on a poster by the bookstore of Sreten J. Djordjević and printed by the State Printing House of the Kingdom of Serbia.

d7bf9369-064f-5991-9f23-3b988f805ff6.name: The Emir Abdelkader, Bey of Mascara in 1807
d7bf9369-064f-5991-9f23-3b988f805ff6.short_description: The Treaty of Tafna was finally signed on 30 May 1837 between General Bugeaud and Emir Abdelkader, a fierce supporter of the armed fight against the French expeditionary corps and of the political and territorial unity of Algeria. This followed a ferocious resistance campaign in the mid-west of the country, marked most notably by the victory at Mazagran. The victories at Mazagran and Sidi-Brahim near Ghazouet in 1745, which resulted in the death of many officers from the French expeditionary, have rarely been depicted by European lithographers, who preferred to focus on Algerian defeats.
d7bf9369-064f-5991-9f23-3b988f805ff6.author: Dalila Orfali

d7c8788d-6f4d-5251-abb7-406fabefb7b2.name: *Napoleon returning from the Island of Elba*
d7c8788d-6f4d-5251-abb7-406fabefb7b2.short_description: Following his abdication in April 1814 due to his defeat at the hands of the coalition between Austria, Prussia and Russia, Napoléon was exiled to Elba, a French territory at the time. He then unexpectedly disembarked at Antibes (France) on 1 March 1815, accompanied by a small army, and went on to take control of Grenoble, Lyon, and finally Paris. King Louis XVIII fled, and Napoléon temporarily regained the throne (the "Hundred Days"), until his defeat at Waterloo marked his final abdication. This image contributed to the myth of Napoléon, illustrating the emperor's determination during his journey from Elba to Paris, also known as the "Vol de l'Aigle" (flight of the eagle).

d815fe5d-36cb-5efe-b0e0-241a5e5e2941.name: Stamp sketch
d815fe5d-36cb-5efe-b0e0-241a5e5e2941.short_description: The Ottoman Empire held a contest to determine the stamp that would be printed in London between 1919 and 1921. Stamp sketches drawn by famous calligraphers are exhibited in the museum. This stamp sketch belonged to the Eminönü Post Office.

d92eefc6-b8cb-57be-9e74-3bd00aa19302.name: *Théâtre de l'Opéra. "Aida". Avenue of the sphinxes at the gates of Thebes (act 2 scene 2)*
d92eefc6-b8cb-57be-9e74-3bd00aa19302.short_description: Commissioned by Isma'il Pasha for the inauguration of the Suez Canal, Verdi's opera *Aida* was performed for the first time in Cairo in 1871, with great success. It recreated life at the time of the pharaohs, with the details and the plot developed by the archaeologist Mariette. *Aida* was performed in Paris from 1876, with a grand and successful performance at the Opéra Garnier in 1880.

d993a25c-fe0f-55cb-b4fb-77d8dd825454.name: *A Room in the Egyptian Museum*
d993a25c-fe0f-55cb-b4fb-77d8dd825454.short_description: The drawing shows the arrangement of Drovetti's collection inside the right wing of the building of the Academy of Sciences in 1852. The wall decoration mimics a wall of green stone tiles. The organisation of this room remained roughly unchanged until 2006. The institution of the Egyptian Museum in Turin marked an essential stage in the rediscovery of Egypt and followed the interpretation of hieroglyphics by Champollion. In 1824 King Carlo Felice of Savoy bought the collection of Egyptian antiquities gathered together by Bernardino Drovetti, general consul of France in Egypt from 1803 to 1830, in order to give to the Piedmontese capital an archaeological museum able to compete with all the other museums around Europe. The Drovetti’s collection was donated to the University Museum together with other Egyptian monuments already part of Savoy's collection. This collection already included more than five thousand pieces including statues (one of them is the famous statue of Rameses II), steles, offering tables, wood and bronze objects, mummies, furniture, jewellery, other materials and a significant number of papyri. A catalogue of the collection was made by Champollion around the 1820s.

d9b9133d-3db3-50b8-9527-532bd887cb5c.name: *The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt and Nubia*, Volume 3, title page: *Temple of El Khasne*
d9b9133d-3db3-50b8-9527-532bd887cb5c.short_description: This image represents the vignette on the title page of Volume 3 to 'The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt and Nubia' from drawings made on the spot by David Roberts, lithographed by Louis Haghe and published in six volumes by F.G. Moon in London between 1842-1845. It is entitled 'Temple of El Khasne, Petra' and shows the spectacular treasury of Petra as seen by travellers approaching the ancient city through the famous, steep and narrow ravine. Petra had remained forgotten until rediscovered by the Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in 1812. Subsequently, it became one of the romantic fascinations of European Orientalist artists and writers.Roberts visited Petra in early March 1839, and he wrote that it was 'probably one of the greatest challenges on earth to a painter'.

d9f215eb-4992-5ee7-b7b8-cde7536471d9.name: *Guisot* (sic): *Sir, do we have to agree to the reforms? Philippe: No! No! No my friend, not even the slightest reform* \[etc.\]
d9f215eb-4992-5ee7-b7b8-cde7536471d9.short_description: Pictured in this cartoon are the King Louis-Philippe and the Head of Government François Guizot. The latter, who in 1848 did not foresee the importance of reform, advised the King to maintain a conservative approach. Since 1847, the opposition to the regime had been getting around the ban on political gatherings by organising banquets. The suppression of one of these banquets triggered the 1848 revolution.

db907e57-774c-5cda-a1a5-d1356aa44b85.name: A plan showing the seats assigned to guests at the gala dinner offered by the Italian King in honour of the Ambassador from Morocco, who visited Italy in June 1890
db907e57-774c-5cda-a1a5-d1356aa44b85.short_description:
In June 1890, the Sultan of Morocco sent an Ambassador to Italy (Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi), to meet the Italian King and present him with extremely rich gifts.  
The Ambassador was received with the highest honours. He met with the Italian Prime Minister and with the King, who offered a gala dinner for him.  
This chart shows that at the gala dinner the Italian King was sitting in front of the Queen. At her right was sitting the Crown Prince and at her left was Ambassador Hagi El Maati el Mazamizi. The Italian Prime Minister and other members of the government participated in the dinner, together with the members of the Ambassador’s escort.
db907e57-774c-5cda-a1a5-d1356aa44b85.author: Giulia Barrera

dbeedf3f-9b7e-5868-aa07-16d65ca3dfc9.short_description: This series of postcards shows the reconstruction of a representative area of the city of Cairo in Milan for the Universal Exhibition of 1906. The Exposition was organised on the occasion of the opening of the Simplon Tunnel in 1906 and covered a space of over a million of square meters. One-third of the area was filled with pavilions designed by famous Italian architects. The exhibition cost was over twelve million lire. The event drew the attention of over five million spectators and the participation of 35 thousand exhibitors.

dc034fc0-8090-5b06-897f-5bcc698817b2.name: Emperor Akbar Receiving a Book
dc034fc0-8090-5b06-897f-5bcc698817b2.short_description:
The emperor is seated with pillow at his back upon an octagonal-shaped and portable throne, under a canopy and at the foot of a tree in an open field. A poet or *mullah* (Muslim priest) presents him with a book. The throne rests upon a floral- patterned Mughal carpet spread over a platform. The emperor is attended by two of his courtiers, two musicians, one with *sitar* (stringed instrument) and one with tambourine; by his falconer who holds a large falcon in his right hand; by an attendant to right of falconer and one to the left, the latter holding a staff; and near him is another mullah. The last four are only partially seen at the base of the platform. The emperor is fanned by a figure behind him. To the immediate left of the emperor stands a servant with a fly-whisk and another holding an unidentified object. All the personages on the carpet except the *mullah* and the two servants are seated. Just above the step to the platform is a dish with a bottle possibly for water with leaf sprays issuing from the mouth, a cup nearby, and at the left corner, a covered cup.  
In the landscape, which extends back to the horizon line, there are two trees and a flowering bush. In the larger tree behind the emperor are two birds. On the horizon line, which is hilly, there is an open wood in the midst of which is a castle.  
The painting is glued down on a thick matboard. The borders (frames) are on a separate piece of paper.
dc034fc0-8090-5b06-897f-5bcc698817b2.dimensions: Image: Length: 22.5cm x Width: 13cm; Sheet: Length: 34.6cm x Height: 23.2cm; Mount (backing board): Length: 41cm x Width: 28.3cm; Mat size: Length: 55.9cm x Width: 40.6cm
dc034fc0-8090-5b06-897f-5bcc698817b2.method_for_datation: The "Akbar-nama" was commissioned in 1590 for Akbar’s minister Abu’l Fazl (died 1602). The manuscript was illustrated with paintings in two separate projects in the later 1590s and in 1604. This painting is likely from the first project. The fine ink and gold border is from the Persian lexicon "Farhang-i-Jahangiri," dated 1608, and was added in the 19th or early 20th century.
dc034fc0-8090-5b06-897f-5bcc698817b2.method_for_provenance: The enthroned figure in this miniature painting is likely the emperor Akbar. He is receiving a copy of the "Akbar-nama" (History of Akbar), an illustrated history of Akbar’s distinguished Mongol ancestry and accomplishments during his long reign. The simple turban, almond-shaped eyes, drooping moustache, sideburns, and distinctive oval-shaped ear all conform to known images of Akbar.
keywords: Emperor; Akbar; Book; Drawing; Watercolor; Ink; Gold; Paper; India; Indian; Asia; watercolour
materials: Ink, opaque watercolor, gold on paper

dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.name: Official Hijaz Railway postcards
dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.short_description: In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line began from Damascus and reached Medina in 1908, never reaching Mecca. The financing for the Hijaz Railway was initially meant to come entirely from charitable donations and in May 1900 Sultan Abdülhamid II began the process with a sizeable donation from his personal funds. Despite national and foreign generosity towards the donations campaign, it soon became clear that this alone was insufficient to raise the funds needed for the construction. Therefore, the government sought to raise funds in many other ways, including the commission of postcards amongst other German-made products, in order to generate further yield. With the title ‘*Vue du chemin-de-fer Hamidié de Hedjaz*’ and with labels in French and Turkish, the postcards depict the construction of the Railway as well as general views and inauguration celebrations. These were available for purchase at local post offices.

deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.name: *Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey* (1784–1839)
deb4b3a7-5e57-5235-b533-346c36e88be2.short_description:
Portrait of Mahmud II, Sultan of Turkey (1784–1839). In 1826 Mahmud II initiated the development of a modern army. This led to the uprising of the Janissary, which was quelled by massacring the rebellious troops. Under Mahmud II's reign, in 1821 the Greeks started their fight for freedom which was granted to them in the Peace of Adrianople in 1829.  
After the destruction of the Janissary, the Ottoman Empire under Sultan Mahmud II had only 35,000 badly trained regular soldiers in 1827. Due to the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt), invaded Syria. On 20 February 1832, the Egyptian Army defeated the Ottoman Army at the Battle of Konya. This forced Mahmud II to sign the Peace of Kütahya and to cede Syria and Kilikia to Egypt.

dec28747-77eb-50f5-a4fc-d8e0b8ada348.name: Print showing a catafalque
dec28747-77eb-50f5-a4fc-d8e0b8ada348.alternate_name: *Castrum Doloris* of Johann Herbart Auersperg in St. Catherine’s Church, Zagreb
dec28747-77eb-50f5-a4fc-d8e0b8ada348.description:
Count Johann Herbart Auersperg was a General and Commander of the Military March. He was a descendant of the old, famous Slovenian Turjak Counts and a brother of Count Weichard, a powerful minister and favourite of the Emperors Ferdinand III and Leopold I. The catafalque was installed in the Jesuit St. Catherine's Church, Zagreb, when Count Johann Herbart Auersperg died in 1669.  
In the centre of the canopied hexagonal base with three steps is the sarcophagus, surrounded by six sculptures of famous Auersperg ancestors. Decorated with numerous candles and symbols in its entirety and signed on the bottom right *IC Mannasser.*  
There are also inscriptions, on the top left in a cartouche held by an angel: *EXCELLMO AC ILLMO ... Anno salut 1669 Aetatis 56* and at the top right in a cartouche held by an angel: *Ipso Die Exequiarum ... moestissimi erexerunt.*  
Following the fashion of European funeral ceremonies also in Croatia, luxurious catafalques were made known as *castrum doloris.* Count Auersperg's social position suggests that a famous Austrian or Italian architect could have staged the funeral ceremony depicted in this print. These architects were in demand at the time to construct various complicated and spectacular performances, usually organised by the Jesuit Order, and designed to enchant the eye and spirit of viewers with the use of impressive effects. A bronze memorial plaque also in the church commemorates Auersperg's death.
dec28747-77eb-50f5-a4fc-d8e0b8ada348.short_description:
A Baroque catafalque was installed in the Jesuit Church of St Catherine, Zagreb for Count Johann Herbart Auersperg, General and Commander of the Military March, who died in 1669. The catafalque shown in this print is typical of a Baroque funeral ceremony of the type staged by the Jesuit Order, and designed to enchant the eye and spirit of viewers with the use of impressive effects.  
A bronze memorial plaque, also in the church, commemorates his death.

Valvasor, Slovenian polymath and collector, had his own mansion museum in Bogenšperg. Scarcity at the end of his life forced him to sell some of his exceptionally valuable holdings, and in 1690, the Zagreb Bishop Aleksandar Mikulić bought his collection of prints and the contents of his library.

dfe6ce78-8f49-57a2-8d22-f6a5967fc725.name: *Constantinople et le Bosphore de Thrace*
dfe6ce78-8f49-57a2-8d22-f6a5967fc725.short_description: With the political developments of 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. Travelling in the 19th century became easier and more reliable due to the advent of steamships and trains. Westerners travelled to the East not only for touristic purposes, but also for scientific research, history, archaeology or for religious reasons. Western travellers told of their experiences and what they saw in eastern countries in their travel books and they even offer advice about the journey. Istanbul, where East and West meet, has been the subject of many a traveller's book.

e18d88ea-cdd3-514a-a77b-17670ead2f02.name: *Jews’ Place of Wailing, Jerusalem*
e18d88ea-cdd3-514a-a77b-17670ead2f02.short_description: The wailing wall is situated at the foot of the western side of the Temple Mount/ Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem, sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims. It has been a site for Jewish prayer and pilgrimage for centuries. From the mid-19th century onwards, several unsuccessful attempts to purchase rights to the wall and its immediate area were made by Jews. With the rise of the Zionist movement in the early 20th century, the wall became a source of friction between the Jewish community and the Muslim religious leadership, who were worried that the wall was being used to further Jewish nationalistic claims to the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif and Jerusalem.This print first appeared (facing p. 140) in 'Walks about the City and Environs of Jerusalem. And: Forty Days in the Desert on the Track of the Israelites, a publication created in two volumnes by the writer and artist W. H. Bartlett and the engraver Ebenezar Challis. The work, based on Bartlett's visit to Jerusalem in the summer of 1842, was first published in London around 1850 by Arthur Hal, Virtue and Co.
e18d88ea-cdd3-514a-a77b-17670ead2f02.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

e19b330e-2bba-52d4-86d4-2f8b8d208303.name: Dr Joseph Hariz, doctoral thesis in medicine
e19b330e-2bba-52d4-86d4-2f8b8d208303.short_description: Pictured here is the cover of a doctoral thesis in medicine written by Joseph Hariz, a Jewish Tunisian doctor at l’Université de Marseille, in 1922. In the early 20th century, the Beylik of Tunis contained 170 qualified doctors, 81 of which were French, 83 were foreigners, and 6 Tunisian, with 2 Muslims and 4 Jews.
e19b330e-2bba-52d4-86d4-2f8b8d208303.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar

e2b48175-dfa4-5317-9f12-0d280735f099.name: Drawing of the railway bridge between the mainland and Venice
e2b48175-dfa4-5317-9f12-0d280735f099.short_description: This panoramic view shows the railway link between Venice and the mainland. In 1837 a company was founded to organize the building of the railway in the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. Construction started in 1840 and the railway reached the Venetian station of Santa Lucia in 1846.

e2eea34e-96fb-5a2d-8d3e-29a6cd5d3d82.name: Carpet Design
e2eea34e-96fb-5a2d-8d3e-29a6cd5d3d82.description: Design of a carpet for its manufacture by the Royal Tapestry Factory of Santa Barbara in Madrid. The manufacturing process of the carpets relies on a previous design. This type of design is not common and the National Museum of Decorative Arts retains several, both from Francisco Javier Amérigo and the former Guild Foundation and is a sample of the manufacturing process that these works were a part of.
e2eea34e-96fb-5a2d-8d3e-29a6cd5d3d82.method_for_datation: Through other similar sets of designs which are signed and contain the seal of the Royal Tapestry Factory.

e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.name: 'The first railway engine in Tripoli'
e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.short_description:
The railway in a colonial context was much more than a means of transport: it was a powerful symbol of modernity, of technological superiority of the colonisers over the colonised, and of mastery over the territory. The construction of railways in colonial situations was often celebrated by the colonialists’ popular press or in postcards, as in this case.  
In Libya, the Italians started building railroads from the first months of colonial rule. The first lines, inaugurated in 1912, connected Tripoli with Ain Zara (11 kms) and to Zanzur (39 kms). By the end of 1915, the railway lines in Libya amounted to 180 kilometres.
e3029e51-8121-5e09-b08a-bd958da4cd09.author: Giulia Barrera

e3d1028e-c33d-53a4-a895-0276547994a0.name: *Construction of the Bordeaux bridge in 1821*
e3d1028e-c33d-53a4-a895-0276547994a0.short_description: The construction of bridges had always been a complicated matter, and particularly so in Bordeaux, where the river was especially temperamental. Until the 19th century people crossed it by ferry. However, in 1810 Napoléon I ordered a bridge to be built in Bordeaux, which was completed in 1822. The expertise this required (particularly the building of tunnels to reduce the size of the structure) attracted the attention of many contemporary engineers and architects.

e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.name: Plan and view of the Holy Sanctuary at Mecca, published by Thomas Tegg, London 1825
e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.short_description: This plate is from George Sale’s translation of the Qur’an. This edition of Sale’s work was published in a two-volume work in 1825, by Thomas Tegg without the Preliminary Discourse or the Memoir of the Translator, which makes up a large part of Sale’s original translation of 1734. The 1734 edition was known to be the first English translation of the Qur’an from the original Arabic. This plate is the same as that in the 1734 edition, and consists of two depictions: ‘*Plan of the Temple of Mecca*’ and ‘*View of the Temple of Mecca*’. It has a key to the significant parts of the Haram and a note stating that the references on both the plan and the view show the same locations. This plan however is missing the signature of the original engraver A.Motte. Hand colour tinting is commonly seen in Tegg’s publishing, however it is rare to find this particular plate from Sale’s *Koran* detached and so finely coloured. It may have been removed, coloured and used as artwork in its own right.
e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.method_for_datation: The date and publication details are included within the book.

e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.name: *Map of the desert between the Nile and the Red Sea, including Mount Zabara \[…\] and the remains of the ancient trade route between Egypt and India*
e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.short_description: The explorer and naturalist Frédéric Cailliaud made significant contributions to the birth of Egyptology thanks to the hieroglyphic tracings he made during his two trips to Egypt (1815–1818; 1819–1822). Muhammad 'Ali Pasha had tasked him with exploring the banks of the Nile and Nubia, where he discovered the monuments and emerald mines of Mount Zabara, and took several tracings from them, which he brought back to France with him. His observations were compiled and published by E.F. Jomard as a sequel to *l'Expedition d'Egypte*.
e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.artist: Author: Frédéric Cailliaud; cartographer: Edme-François Jomard; engraver: Alexandre Blondeau

e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.name: Portrait of David Roberts, Esq., R. A.
e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.short_description: This engraving shows a portrait of David Roberts (1796 – 1864), first completed in the 1840s by Charles Baugniet. Roberts is shown seated on an ancient plinth or capital, holding a drawing board and a pencil. A classical temple structure appears in the background on the left. David Roberts was a Scottish painter especially known for a prolific series of detailed lithograph prints of Egypt and the Near East produced during the 1840s from sketches he made during extensive tours of the region (1838–1839). These, and his large oil paintings of similar subjects, made him a prominent and highly influential Orientalist painter. Charles-Louis Baugniet (1814 - 1886), was a Belgian artist famous for the lithographing of portraits of prominent European figures.
e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
e532dd30-df15-5462-88cf-6f2eaa8cf7bd.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

e5dcb5be-a7f2-5f24-b1e8-fae35ee4b7b5.name: *Foundations of Haram al-Sharif*
e5dcb5be-a7f2-5f24-b1e8-fae35ee4b7b5.short_description: Foundations of the South-Eastern corner of the Haram es-Sharif, as revealed for the first time by Charles Warren. This tunnel was some 85 feet below ground. Warren’s team were experienced mining engineers, and were assisted, as shown in several of this sequence of watercolours by William ‘Crimea’ Simpson, sent to record the expedition for the Illustrated London News, by extremely courageous local Jerusalem residents.

e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.name: *Holy Trinity Column in Buda*
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.description:
In the 17th and 18th centuries, different types of Holy Trinity statues reminded people of the sufferings of the plague of 1691. The Holy Trinity Column in Buda, standing in front of the Parish Church of the Holy Virgin and the Old Town House of Buda, was built between 1710 and 1714. In 1916, during World War I, the column was the scene of the coronation of king Charles IV Habsburg. The column was demolished at the end of the 19th century.  
The original copperplates for this engraving are also preserved in the museum's collection. There were nine statues on the monument altogether, all of which were carved by Fülöp (Philipp) Ungleich. The three reliefs and coat-of arms were made by Antal (Anton) Hörger. Later, 16 statues were added to the column. The architectural setting surrounding the column also changed several times. During World War II the original statues in the collection of the Budapest History Museum were seriously damaged. A smaller size engraving was also made of the monument decades later.
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.short_description: A large-size Baroque engraving representing the Holy Trinity Column, one of Buda’s most precious Baroque monuments.
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.method_for_datation: On the basis of the work and its inscription
e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.obtention: Transferred from the Capital’s collection in 1945

e675bda3-74cc-5e0b-82fb-22ec48a324a5.author: Beatrix Basics

e6775e8c-d02b-5493-bf5e-5bcf66f6cbb0.name: ‘*A Short Note on the Design and Issue of Postage Stamps Prepared by the Survey of Egypt for His Highness Husein Emir & Sherif of Mecca & King of the Hejaz*’
e6775e8c-d02b-5493-bf5e-5bcf66f6cbb0.short_description: Prepared for ‘His Highness Husein. Emir & Sherif of Mecca & King of the Hejaz’, this detailed work with an unsigned introduction by Sir Henry MacMahon, details the creation of new postage stamps following on from independence from Ottoman rule. It also describes the design and technical attributions of the stamps, in detail. T.E. Lawrence conducted his initial research on the stamp issue by exploring design motifs in museums and buildings in Cairo. He drew inspiration from monuments such as from the tomb of al-Ghuri and the prayer niche of the mosque of al-Amri and from manuscripts such as Sultan Barquq’s Qur’an, amongst others. In his letters, T.E.Lawrence notes his fascination of the project, at one point suggesting that flavoured gum be used on the reverse of the stamps, to make them less unpleasant. Colonel Cyril Wilson (1873-1938) is now thought to be the main driving force behind the Arab Revolt of 1916-1918. He had an important diplomatic role which was connected to the safe passage of British Muslim pilgrims from India. This was in order to maintain control in Arabia and prevent any disruptions from rebel groups keen to spread anti-British sentiment.
e6775e8c-d02b-5493-bf5e-5bcf66f6cbb0.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
e6775e8c-d02b-5493-bf5e-5bcf66f6cbb0.method_for_datation: Information on publisher and date is included in the book.

e696126e-a8d7-5829-87b8-1372eb83e64c.name: A book on the activities of the Italian community in Tunisia, published by the Italian Chamber of Commerce of Tunisia for the 1906 International Exhibition in Milan
e696126e-a8d7-5829-87b8-1372eb83e64c.short_description:
In 1906, in celebration of the Simplon Tunnel opening between Italy and Switzerland, the Italian government organised an international exhibition in Milan. On that occasion, Italian communities in Egypt and Tunisia published books that described their lives and activities.  
In Tunisia, Italians entrepreneurs and professionals set up a committee charged with organising the participation to the exhibition of the Italian community in Tunisia.
e696126e-a8d7-5829-87b8-1372eb83e64c.author: Giulia Barrera

e6b696c1-80fd-5fd5-8b33-a15b88ca3ccb.name: An Italian Pasta Factory in Tunisia
e6b696c1-80fd-5fd5-8b33-a15b88ca3ccb.short_description: According to historian Adriano Salmieri, in 1921 the four Tunisian towns of Tunis, Sfax, Sousse (Susa) and Bizerte had a total of 133 Italian shops making pasta and bread. Making pasta was hard work. In Tunisia, the industrialization of pasta production started only in the 20th century.
e6b696c1-80fd-5fd5-8b33-a15b88ca3ccb.author: Giulia Barrera

e6ce0745-bf5d-5a64-ab65-c5f97224e8ef.name: The Hall of Greece donated by the Greek government to the city of Rome, Rome Exhibition, 1911
e6ce0745-bf5d-5a64-ab65-c5f97224e8ef.short_description: On the occasion of the International Exhibition of Rome in 1911, the complex of the "Baths of Diocletian” was restored under the direction of the archeologist and topographer Rodolfo Lanciani. The site housed the Archaeological Exhibition dedicated to the Roman culture in the Imperial Era with a particular interest for its positive influence on the ex provinces. Every single nation participated through original reproductions of archaeological materials, often lost. The photo shows material evidence and casts coming from Greece.

e6f49abd-8e7a-5131-a593-cada7ee6ab5e.name: Interior of Cattan's Bazaar; Interior of the Pavilion of Abdallah Ben Athia; Interior of the Eskenazi Museum of Antiquities [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
e6f49abd-8e7a-5131-a593-cada7ee6ab5e.short_description: International Exhibition in Paris, 1878. Tunisia is represented by the creation of different bazaars. The reporter's descriptions of Cattan's Bazaar report mainly religious objects such as wooden rosary beads, mother-pearl crosses and the biblical plant, the Rose of Jericho. The Ben Athia Bazaar displayed cultural objects from Tunisia: luxury arms, rich materials, embroidery, perfumes of roses, bronze and enamelled jewellery. The Eskenazi bazaar displayed various antique objects.

e714183d-faa1-5c38-bf56-e05a8f41f61e.short_description: This copy of a beautiful watercolour from Charles Lallemand's book *Tunis et ses Environs* shows the Porte de la Mer, or the Porte de France, around which both European settlers and Tunisian residents are gathered. Its location was strategic, as it led to both the Tunis medina and the European quarter.

e751862b-fe57-57d5-ba9b-2d07b6938bd0.short_description: Italian anti-colonial cartoon, with a clear socialist imprint: according to the author, soldiers of both sides were equal victims of the war, while businessmen of both sides made profits out of the war.

e76382a2-64c9-5d5c-8c41-049ddd06c52d.name: Newspaper *al-Hoda*
e76382a2-64c9-5d5c-8c41-049ddd06c52d.short_description: These two issues of *al-Hoda* date to 12 October 1901 and 27 November 1901. *Al-Hoda* was a semi-weekly critical periodical founded by N. A. Mokarzel and written, edited and printed in Philadelphia, USA.
e76382a2-64c9-5d5c-8c41-049ddd06c52d.holder: House of the Maronite Patriarchate of Antioch and all the East
